News.title: Bride holds wedding without groom after being jilted seven days before saying 'I do'
News.content:
Glass of bubbly in hand, glancing over at her beautiful white gown, this was not the wedding day Katherine Jones had expected. Despite 18 months of meticulous planning, one major element was missing … the groom. Seven days before their three day wedding celebration in Tuscany, Italy, her partner of six-and-half years told her: “I just feel like we shouldn’t get married.”

Katherine, 36, says: “Remembering those eight devastating words, my eyes fill up.” But she decided to host her Tuscan wedding without him. She says: “I may not be getting married today, but there is going to be a party, complete with wedding dress, bridesmaids and toasts to the bride. It will still be my big day.”

Meeting Alex (not his real name) online when she was 30 and he was 31, they clicked immediately. She says: “He was handsome and ambitious, a fellow business owner, and had a calm that balanced out my own more frenetic energy. Within months we were in love and after a year had moved in together.”

Will.i.am shares plan for new show combining The Voice and The Apprentice READ MORE :

View 8 Images Katherine Jones getting ready for her wedding day (Image: Simone Trebbi Studio)

‌



Liked by her family and friends, four happy years followed, travelling, socialising and buying a three-bedroom detached house in Liverpool. Then, in 2024, Katherine lost £50,000 in a business scam and worked 24/7 to make the money back. But cracks started forming in her relationship.

Normally the upbeat, problem solver, she was stressed and vulnerable, saying: “It was as if our relationship didn’t work if I wasn’t the cheerleader for us both.” If she fixed her business problems, she believed they would be happy again.

And, on New Years Eve 2024, on a beach in Thailand, Alex proposed. She says: “It was a beautiful moment and I didn’t hesitate to say yes.” Choosing Tuscany for their wedding, she says: “We both loved Italy. I spent a lot of time there due to my business, the ThinK Wine Group, (MUST INCLUDE) which imports my wines from Italy. “

View 8 Images L-R The jilted bride's sister, mum, Katherine, auntie, and other sister on her wedding day (Image: Simone Trebbi Studio)

‌



Searching for the perfect venue together, she adds: “It was so romantic, and I’d never felt more connected to Alex.” Their wedding idyll was set high in the Tuscan hills. She says: “It had a church for the ceremony, grounds that included a pool and enough space for all fifty guests to stay.” There they would enjoy three days, with a welcome dinner, wedding day feast and a next-day pool party.

While they picked the suits and rings together, Katherine was left to do virtually everything else. But choosing her wedding gown with her mum, sisters and auntie in October 2025 was magical. When the sight of her in one gorgeous long sleeved lace gown made her auntie cry, she says: “I felt transformed.”

At work, however, she went through three months of non-stop stress. And she confronted Alex, saying: “‘ I feel so alone and you’re not supporting me. What’s going on?’” He replied: “I’m not happy with how things are between us.”

View 8 Images L-R Sister of the jilted bride , mum, Katherine Jones and her other sister on her wedding day (Image: Simone Trebbi Studio)

‌



Relieved by his honesty, but panicked, she replied, saying: “‘Oh my god, we’re getting married in seven months!’ ‘‘I know,’ he said, clearly upset. ‘We need to spend time together and really work on our relationship.’” So they did - soon growing close again, while the wedding plans - which were costing thousands - continued.

But when Alex returned from his stag do in Scotland in early July, she says: “I sensed something had changed.” Distant and reluctant to talk, Katherine thought Alex’s shyness may mean he was nervous about the imminent ceremony.

A few weeks later, she spent four days at a residential boot camp to shed a few pounds before the wedding. On her return, he was cold and distant - and had left before she awoke the following day. She says: “At 9pm, Alex eventually returned, his expression still stormy.

View 8 Images Jilted bride Katherine Jones in her white jumpsuit at her wedding celebrations

‌



“‘What’s wrong?’ I said, hearing my voice wobble. ‘I deserve to know.’ Finally, sitting at the kitchen table and refusing to meet my eyes, he said quietly ‘I just feel like we shouldn’t get married.’ “I truly thought I was about to be sick, nausea fighting with heartbreak as I began to cry. 'But we’re getting married next week,’ I managed to say. He still refused to look at me. Finally came a flood of anger. ‘Why the hell didn’t you tell me this before?’ I demanded. ‘How dare you put me through this?’”

Alex said he’d been unhappy since December. Katherine considered begging him to change his mind, but dignity and good sense prevailed. She says: “I could never marry a man who could do this to me. Despite the rollercoaster of emotions, I knew one thing for sure. Groom or no groom, I was going to Italy. The venue was paid in full, the guests had all booked their flights. We wouldn’t get a penny of our deposits back. So this event was happening, with or without him.”

She even drove, sobbing, to her final dress fitting the next day. She says: “Seeing myself in the gown that had made me feel so beautiful just a few months before was unbearable.”

View 8 Images The impressive table for Katherine's wedding feast (Image: Simone Trebbi Studio)

‌



Meeting her mum and sister afterwards she told them, tearfully, she wanted to proceed with the party, but only wanted the 30 friends and family on her side. She couldn’t face being reminded of Alex by his guests.

Totally supportive, her loved ones took charge, telling all concerned. Katherine says: “Time only passed thanks to wine, Mum staying with me in the day and my friends coming over at night. I hugely appreciated their love and support.”

Meanwhile, Alex moved into their converted garage, her questions and accusations of cowardice met with apologies, but not answers. She says: “I was exhausted, heartbroken and furious, but I had a wedding day to get to.”

Unable to face collecting her bridal gown, she packed her more casual dress, her white party jumpsuit, the robe she had bought for her wedding morning and the white swimsuit for the pool party - but immediately removed her engagement ring. She confesses: “My bravado lasted until I arrived at the venue on 29 July, where I broke down. Despite my tears, looking out at the perfect Tuscan view I told myself, ‘I’d rather be here than back at home sobbing in bed. I’m going to make the most of every minute.’”

‌



View 8 Images Jilted bride Katherine Jones shows off a dress from her wedding wardrobe

Asking her friends and family not to talk about what had happened, instead she asked them to make her laugh. She adds: “For three days we ate, drank and danced. From the delicious welcome meal and the lovely speeches and toasts at the reception, to the brilliant pool party, everything was exactly as I’d planned it - minus the ceremony and groom.

“The hardest moment came when it was all over and everyone left. I cried all day, a mixture of sadness and relief.” Then she honeymooned on the Amalfi Coast - with her mum, instead of her husband.

As for the inevitable gossip? She says: “I refused to be ashamed about being jilted. I’d done nothing wrong, so why should I hide away? “To address the gossip head on, I decided to post a TikTok video about it.”

‌



View 8 Images Jilted bride Katherine enjoys a cocktail on her honeymoon without her groom

Aimed for people she knew, she continues: “Within hours my follower count was into the thousands and messages began pouring in. Women told me how they wished they’d cancelled their wedding, or enjoyed it without their groom, as they’d gone ahead despite obvious relationship problems. How happy they were I was speaking openly about it. Within five days, I had more than 75,000 followers.”

Delighted by the response, Katherine now hopes to inspire other jilted brides to reclaim their wedding experience. She says: “I honestly don’t know what’s going to happen in the months to come, how Alex and I will disentangle our lives or what it will be like to begin a new chapter. I’m so thankful we didn’t get married. My solo wedding has proved to me I’m strong enough to do anything alone.”

* Follow Katherine on TikTok at @kathjay89

News.title: Millions on 4 benefits must act by Sunday to secure £150 boost
News.content:
Millions on 4 benefits must act by Sunday to secure £150 boost

The government has issued a reminder to eligible households to check they are named on their energy bill

View Image People on some benefits can get a boost to help with energy bills this winter (Image: Getty)

Energy customers have just days left until Sunday to secure a £150 payment delivered directly into their accounts. Households must act by 23 August or risk missing out entirely.

‌



Approximately six million households will receive the rebate this winter, with roughly 250,000 in Scotland getting it automatically for the first time. Yet the Andy Burnham government has encouraged eligible households to verify they're named on their bill to receive the Warm Home Discount automatically.

‌



This comes after the Prime Minister's swift decision to scrap VAT on domestic electricity bills from 1 October as one of his earliest actions in office, knocking £45 off the annual Ofgem price cap. Officials said the reminder follows immediate measures to eliminate VAT from electricity bills from 1 October, providing households with cost-of-living relief.

‌



Those claiming means-tested benefits automatically qualify for the Warm Home Discount, provided they're listed as their household's energy bill payer. Their name must appear on the energy bill by 23 August to access the support, so checking now and making any required amendments is advisable.

On Wednesday Ofgem will announce its quarterly energy price cap for the period October 1 to December 31. Household energy prices are set increase again to the highest level for three years heading into winter, according to new forecasts.

Bills are due to increase despite the Prime Minister’s plan to remove VAT from household electricity bills from October. The energy price cap is currently expected to increase by 4% in October compared with the current rate, experts at Cornwall Insight said.

‌



For the £150 bonus, eligible customers using pre-payment meters who top up with a key or card will also need to confirm their household's account is registered under their name. Energy customers have been informed that 24 firms have joined a scheme delivering millions a £150 payment straight into their accounts.

Every household where the billpayer receives means-tested benefits qualifies for the rebate. In England and Wales, those receiving Housing Benefit, Income-related Employment and Support Allowance, Pension Credit and Universal Credit will be eligible – the same group as last winter.

What benefits are covered?

‌



The government says around six million households are in line to receive the discount after the scheme was expanded last year.

In England and Wales, households in receipt of the following benefits are eligible:

Housing benefit

Income-related employment and support allowance

Pension credit

Universal credit

‌



In Scotland, around 250,000 households will get the payment automatically for the first time.

They need to be claiming either:

Pension credit

The extra amount of universal credit for a child or due to a disability

A disability or pensioner premium of income-related employment support allowance

A disability or pensioner premium and have a support for a mortgage interest loan

Have a child under five and are unemployed and get universal credit, or income-related employment support allowance or a support or mortgage interest loan.

‌



Energy bills have already risen by 13% this summer, and a further 4% hike is expected later in the year.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said: "Families will be worried about their energy bills this winter and our focus is on giving them breathing space, as we continue to work to bring down bills. Almost a million more families with children received the £150 Warm Home Discount last winter, after we expanded scheme.

"If you know someone who might benefit, please start spreading the word and encourage them to check they are named on their energy bill. ".

‌



The government is urging eligible households to verify they are named on their electricity bill, with providers set to rely on customers' records as of Sunday 23 August.

Someone may not be listed on their electricity bill if they have recently relocated. Eligible customers using pre-payment meters who top up with a key or card must also ensure their household account is registered under their name.

Earlier this year, the government confirmed that millions of qualifying households will continue to receive the Warm Home Discount right through to 2030/1, securing the scheme for the remainder of the decade.

‌



Last year's Budget delivered an average saving of £150 on energy bills, a reduction that has already been built into future billing calculations. The government also stated that the Warm Homes Plan is designed to cut energy consumption, slash bills for millions of households and help tackle fuel poverty across the country.

Cornwall said it expected a typical household to be facing an annual bill of £1,729, from October, up from £1,663, based on an Ofgem’s updated definition of a typical consumer, which came into effect from July to reflect falling household energy use.

It said this would be the equivalent of £1,941 per year based on its previous calculations, up from £1,862 currently. It would mark the highest average bill since July 2023.

‌



The increased October cap, which will remain in place for three months, will come into force as households start to increase their energy usage further by using their heating more regularly, adding to bills.

The following suppliers will be part of the winter 2026 to 2027 scheme:

100Green (formerly Green Energy UK or GEUK)

Boost

British Gas

E - also known as E (Gas and Electricity)

Ecotricity

EDF

EnergyCoop – see Octopus Energy

E.ON Next

Fuse Energy

Good Energy

Home Energy

London Power

Octopus Energy

Outfox Energy

OVO

Sainsbury’s Energy

Scottish Gas – see British Gas

ScottishPower

So Energy

Square 1 Energy Ltd

TruEnergy

Tulo Energy

Utilita

Utility Warehouse

‌



Cornwall said the expected increase in October will be less than otherwise expected because of the proposed removal of VAT from household electricity bills.

The Prime Minister previously said this would knock around £45 off the annual Ofgem price cap from October.

However, the experts said the recent swing in global energy prices has more than offset the downward impact of the VAT policy.

‌



Dr Craig Lowrey, principal consultant at Cornwall Insight, said: “Rising energy bills aren’t welcome at the best of times, but with winter approaching this latest hike will hit struggling households especially hard.

“Driven by international conflict rather than domestic policy, it is a stark reminder that our energy bills remain tied to events thousands of miles away.

“Moments like this are the strongest argument for reducing Britain’s reliance on volatile international gas.

‌



“While temporary relief like VAT cuts help soften the blow, they don’t touch the underlying fact that Britain is heavily dependent on imports of natural gas.”

A Government spokesman said: “Tackling the cost of living remains a key priority for this Government and we know families will be worried by the prospect of higher energy bills this winter.

“We’re acting to give consumers breathing space with the cost of living – cutting VAT on energy bills, ensuring around six million households get the £150 warm home discount this winter, and making millions of homes cheaper to run through our warm homes plan.

Article continues below

“Alongside our efforts to support rapid de-escalation in the Middle East, we will do everything we can to shield consumers from global energy shocks and bring down bills for good.”

News.title: ‘I got cancer at 26 - it opened doors I never expected’
News.content:
‘I got cancer at 26 - it opened doors I never expected’

Jordan Loydall is urging young people to 'trust their instincts' after his shock diagnosis

View 3 Images Jordan Loydall never expected that someone his age could get kidney cancer (Image: Jordan Loydall)

Jordan Loydall ran 101 kilometres in March 2026 raising over £1,600 for Kidney Cancer UK barely two years after being diagnosed with stage 2 kidney cancer but the real shock of his diagnosis was the impact it had on his career. The 27-year-old hopes to spread awareness as he didn’t realise the disease could affect people as young as he was. He told the charity: “If my story helps even one person trust their instincts, seek medical advice, or feel less alone after a diagnosis, then it’s worth telling.”

‌



In 2024, Jordan had been dismissing some of his early symptoms as the side effects of having two bulging discs in his spine. The then-26-year-old went for an MRI where one out of 53 images showed a lump on his kidney.

‌



With reassurances from his doctors that cancer was unlikely, Jordan was floored when he got his diagnosis that December. He recalled: “My parents and my now fiancé were in the room with me when the doctor told us the news.

‌



“I’ve always been someone who worries about the people around me, so my first thoughts weren’t really about myself; they were about how my family would cope with hearing that I had cancer.”

View 3 Images His diagnosis and recovery gave Jordan a new perspective on his career (Image: Jordan Loydall)

Jordan, from Newport, South Wales, had the cancerous part of his kidney removed in February 2025 and while the operation was a success, the recovery would change his life in ways the 26-year-old never expected.

‌



He shared: “I suddenly lost a lot of my independence. I needed help with things that I normally would have done myself, like getting out of bed or up and down the stairs, and it made me feel completely useless.

“At times, I felt like I was a burden on the people looking after me, even though in reality, I wasn’t. My family and friends were incredibly supportive, but accepting help was something I had to learn.”

His recovery meant time away from work in a graduate scheme at a telecoms company. The shock of his situation paired with space away from his work gave him an unexpected new perspective as he realised how unhappy he was.

‌



Growing up in a family of tradespeople, he decided to pursue a Health & Safety qualification. Today, he works in local government as a Health, Safety and Wellbeing Officer, supporting primary schools.

He said: “I’m now in a job I absolutely love. Sometimes, life events that feel devastating at the time can also open doors you never expected.”

With some psychological support, Jordan soon realised he’d spent so much time worrying about others that he hadn’t processed his own emotions about his diagnosis. Now on the otherside of his recovery, and career changes, the 27-year-old has turned his attention to more philanthropic ventures.

‌



In March 2026, he finished what he described as the hardest, but most rewarding, challenge of his life; running a total of 101 kilometres throughout the month and raising £1,645 for Kidney Cancer UK.

View 3 Images Kidney cancer affects thousands of people in the UK (Image: GETTY)

He said: “As I learned more about the charity and the incredible support they provide to people affected by kidney cancer, I became passionate about helping to raise awareness of the disease and supporting their important work.

Article continues below

“If my story helps even one person trust their instincts, seek medical advice, or feel less alone after a diagnosis, then it’s worth telling.”

News.title: Adding £1.50 item to lasagne while cooking makes it taste 'next level'
News.content:
Adding £1.50 item to lasagne while cooking makes it taste 'next level'

A simple kitchen staple can transform a classic Italian comfort dish into a restaurant-quality feast

View 3 Images Better tasting lasagna every time when this is added while cooking (Image: ©2023 Wayne Wilson)

Lasagne is already one of those dishes that can make a kitchen smell like a restaurant, but there is a surprisingly simple way to give the sauce another layer of flavour. The trick involves a small amount of an ingredient that some cooks might not expect to find anywhere near a beef ragù.

‌



Anchovy paste can be stirred into the sauce to add savoury depth without turning the finished dish into something that tastes strongly of fish. Anchovies are naturally rich in umami, the savoury taste often associated with foods such as meat, cheese and mushrooms.

‌



Food researchers at the University of Reading have studied umami and flavour enhancement, with research showing how naturally occurring compounds can contribute to stronger savoury characteristics. The university describes umami as the fifth basic taste and has specifically researched ways of using umami-rich ingredients to improve flavour.

‌



The idea is already used in British cooking. BBC Good Food recommends adding a touch of anchovy to meat sauces for extra saltiness, while its anchovy guide describes the ingredient as a way of adding a salty, umami flavour to sauces and dressings.

How to use anchovy paste in lasagne

View 3 Images Restaurant-quality lasagna (Image: Getty Images)

You do not need much to make a difference. A small spoonful can be added while cooking the onion and garlic, or stirred through the meat sauce as it cooks.

‌



The important part is giving it time to cook into the sauce. British food website Abel & Cole uses anchovies in its beef ragù, adding them after the vegetables have softened and cooking them briefly before the wine, stock and tomato passata go in.

It should break down into the sauce rather than remain as obvious pieces. BBC Good Food similarly demonstrates anchovies dissolving during cooking in its umami gravy recipe.

View 3 Images Anchovies, but not in paste form (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

That makes it a useful option for cooks who want more depth without adding another bulky ingredient to the lasagne. It is worth remembering, however, that anchovies are salty, so the finished sauce should be tasted before adding additional salt.

Anchovy is not limited to lasagne, either. Great British Chefs has highlighted anchovy paste for its umami contribution in barbecue sauce, while Abel & Cole uses anchovies in a slow-cooked beef ragù.

So if the next batch of lasagne tastes like it is missing something, a little anchovy paste could be worth trying. Used sparingly and cooked into the ragù, it can provide the savoury boost without requiring a complicated change to a favourite recipe.

News.title: Royal Mail customers told to do one this before looking for missing parcels
News.content:
Royal Mail customers told to do one this before looking for missing parcels

It can be frustrating to come home to find a parcel hasn't been delivered

View Image Royal Mail customers may be able to easily find their parcel (Image: Liudmila Chernetska via Getty Images)

Waiting for an important parcel that fails to turn up can be incredibly frustrating.

‌



Fortunately, Royal Mail has outlined precisely what you should do if your delivery hasn't arrived. And the good news is it doesn't mean hunting around the house or garden. Rather than searching in designated 'safe' spots or knocking on your neighbours' doors, you can simply use Royal Mail's 'Track your item' tool to find out exactly where your parcel is and when it's due to arrive.

‌



The expected delivery time for your parcel or letter will depend on which service was used to send it. The 'Track your item' feature lets you check the most up-to-date information on items sent via signed for or tracked services.

‌



Simply enter your reference number – which will be between 9-27 characters long – found on your Post Office receipt and the label indicating the service used. If you're the recipient, the sender will be able to provide this for you.

If a tracked or signed for service wasn't used and your item still hasn't shown up, different rules apply. Royal Mail aims to deliver all 1st Class mail by the next working day, and all 2nd Class mail within two to three working days.

Article continues below

Should the item remain undelivered beyond the due date plus 10 working days, the sender might be able to claim for compensation. If you're the recipient, you'll need to get in touch with the sender, who can then contact Royal Mail directly to make enquiries on your behalf.

If a postal worker tries to deliver your parcel but is unsuccessful – for instance, if there's no one at home – you should receive a P739 card, which means you'll need to collect the item from the sorting office yourself. Depending on when you spot the card, this could mean waiting until the next day.

In certain circumstances, however, it may be possible to arrange a redelivery instead.

News.title: Bruce Forsyth's widow now as beautiful mansion they once shared 'left to rot'
News.content:
Bruce Forsyth's widow now as beautiful mansion they once shared 'left to rot'

Bruce Forsyth's former Wentworth mansion, once shared with widow Lady Wilnelia, has reportedly been left empty and deteriorating years after she sold it for £5.7million

View 4 Images Bruce Forsyth died aged 89 (Image: PA)

Bruce Forsyth's widow Lady Wilnelia has moved on from the lavish Surrey mansion she shared with the TV legend, but the once-glamorous property has reportedly been left abandoned.

‌



The sprawling home, known as Straidarran, sits on the exclusive Wentworth Estate, where huge mansions owned by celebrities, sports stars and wealthy international buyers line the private roads.

‌



Bruce lived at the property for decades before his death in 2017, aged 89, following a battle with bronchial pneumonia. Three years later, in April 2020, Wilnelia, 68, sold the mansion to a Bermuda-based businesswoman for a reported £5.7million.

‌



But despite the hefty price tag, there appears to have been little visible activity at the property since the sale.

What Strictly professionals really think of new presenting line-up READ MORE :

View 4 Images Lady Wilnelia Forsyth and Sir Bruce had been married since 1983 (Image: PA)

Locals say the home has been left largely untouched, with no obvious signs of residents or major refurbishment work.

‌



Once the setting for Bruce and Wilnelia's glamorous life, the mansion came packed with luxury features including a ten-seat cinema, swimming pool, tennis court, gym, library and wine cellar.

The gates still bear an "F" crest associated with Forsyth's surname, while warning signs have been erected around the property.

One local said the situation was particularly unusual because overseas buyers on the estate often demolish older properties and replace them with new-build mansions.

‌



"Normally overseas owners on the estate knock these old homes down and build a new one. So it is a very strange situation with Bruce's old home, where seemingly nothing has happened since Wilnelia sold it six years ago," they told The Sun.

The source claimed the only noticeable change had been the arrival of security following break-ins. They added: "The only thing I have noticed is that security is present there, the owners certainly aren't, but that only followed break-ins."

View 4 Images The mansion was located on the Wentworth estate but has been left empty (Image: w8media)

‌



Security was reportedly stepped up after urban explorers targeted the property, with police confirming reports of break-ins to the publication.

Wentworth Estate manager James Perotin previously said the mansion was now being monitored around the clock. He said: "Security has been increased at Bruce Forsyth's old house, there is now a van permanently on site, and it is monitored 24 hours a day."

Perotin also suggested that some wealthy homeowners on the estate spend much of their time abroad, partly because of tax reasons, leaving some properties unoccupied for years.

‌



Wilnelia, meanwhile, downsized after selling the family mansion and bought another home on the same estate for around £3million. The former beauty queen and Bruce were married in 1983 and remained together until his death.

Bruce, who entertained generations of viewers, became a household name through shows including The Generation Game and Play Your Cards Right, before becoming the face of Strictly Come Dancing. He presented the BBC dance show for a decade before stepping down in 2014.

Wilnelia, originally from Puerto Rico, was crowned Miss World in 1975. The couple shared a son, Jonathan Joseph, now 40, with Bruce's entire estimated £15million fortune being left to his third wife rather than his six children.

‌



In 2018, Wilnelia spoke about the final days she spent with Bruce before his death. She said she felt "lucky" that all the close family members managed to say goodbye.

In December, Tess Daly held back tears as Wilnelia sent her and Claudia Winkleman a sweet message before their Strictly Come Dancing exit. It was shown during the spin off show It Takes Two.

View 4 Images Wilnelia sold the mansion in 2020 (Image: Jonathan Buckmaster)

‌



Tess had presented Strictly alongside Bruce from the show's launch in 2004, with Claudia taking over in 2013. "Hello Tess and Claudia," Wilnelia told the hosts.

"Sending you both my warmest wishes as you step into this exciting new chapter. Tess, you shared so many wonderful years on Strictly with Bruce and I know he would be so proud of you."

She continued: "And Claudia, your sparkle and wit have brought so much joy to everyone. Thank you both for the laughter, the elegance and the heart you have given to the show.

Article continues below

"All my love and the very best for the future ahead." Signing off on her husband's famous catchphrase, she said: "Don't forget, life is too short, so... keep dancing!" Tess replied: "What a woman! She's just a goddess."

News.title: NHS worker drove wrong way down M61 slip road to avoid traffic jam
News.content:
NHS worker drove wrong way down M61 slip road to avoid traffic jam

A motorist is prosecuted every week for risking a head-on collision by reckless drivers who are caught reversing along the motorway, shocking research has found

View 2 Images He could now face a driving ban (Image: GMP/PA Wire)

An NHS worker who was caught driving the wrong way down a motorway slip road could be banned from driving.

Innocent Ayodele, 32, an NHS worker from Manchester, was caught trying to escape a traffic jam on the M61 by driving the wrong way up an entry slip road.

Appearing in court in May he apologised for his actions. Pc Peter Weatherstone, from Greater Manchester Police (GMP), told Preston Magistrates’ Court he spoke to Ayodele to ask “what he was playing at driving the wrong way”.

“I could see another driver at the side of another vehicle whom he could have struck”, he wrote in his statement. “I pointed out the dangers of such behaviour, but the driver seemed totally blatant in his necessary to do this simply because he had finished worked and wanted to get home.”

View 2 Images In June, National Highways data obtained by the Press Association revealed that 947 incidents involving “oncoming vehicles” on England’s motorways had been logged in the 12 months to May 11. (Image: Getty Images)

Drug kingpin jailed after fleeing to Dubai and five years on the run READ MORE :

Ayodele told the curt he was trying to get home to his pregnant wife, but with nine penalty points already on his licence he could now face a ban when he is sentenced at a later date.

It comes as research has revealed that a motorist gets prosecuted every week for risking a head-on collision by driving the wrong way on the motorway. Reckless drivers are caught reversing along the carriageway, pulling U-turns next to high-speed traffic and driving backwards in a bid to reach a missed exit junction, court papers show.

The Press Association has found that 31 drivers in the past 30 weeks were charged by police with criminal offences involving driving in the wrong direction on the motorways of England and Wales. Those convicted are typically ordered to pay out hundreds of pounds in fines and court fees while some face driving bans as a result of their actions.

In June, National Highways data obtained by the Press Association revealed that 947 incidents involving “oncoming vehicles” on England’s motorways had been logged in the 12 months to May 11.

News.title: Woman dies after plummeting from 18th floor of hotel in popular tourist spot
News.content:
Woman dies after plummeting from 18th floor of hotel in popular tourist spot

The woman's husband alerted hotel staff and he tearfully said his wife had done something "outrageous" - he has reportedly been arrested

View 3 Images The incident occurred at the Breathless Cancun Soul Resort

A woman has died after falling from the 18th floor of a hotel in Mexico.

The incident occurred at the Breathless Cancun Soul Resort in Cancun on the night of Thursday, August 20.

The woman's husband alerted hotel staff. According to reports, he tearfully told staff that his wife had done something "outrageous".

The American woman and her husband are understood to have been guests at the hotel.

View 3 Images The incident took place in Cancun, Mexico (Image: ELIZABETH RUIZ, AFP via Getty Images)

Cancun is a popular holiday spot on the northeast coast of the Yucatan Peninsula in Quintana Roo, Mexico. It is known for its crystal-clear waters.

Hotel security rushed to the scene and found that the woman had fallen around 150ft (over 45 metres).

Emergency services were called to the hotel and the woman was pronounced dead at the scene.

A police investigation has been opened into the tragic death.

View 3 Images A police investigation has been opened into the tragic death (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

The Mail reported that her husband was arrested.

News of the incident comes one month after a British tourist drowned after being swept away by strong waves while in the same resort town.

Article continues below

The man, 60, who was swimming with his children at San Miguelito beach.

He reportedly got into difficulty after entering the water despite a red flag warning.

His two children were rescued, but he was pulled from the sea unconscious and pronounced dead at the scene.

News.title: Girl, 6, dies days after Shoreham sea tragedy killed three family members
News.content:
A six-year-old girl has died in hospital after getting into difficulty in the sea off Shoreham in West Sussex, in an incident which also killed her father, mother and sister.

Saja El-Khawas, a British Palestinian from London, was pulled from the sea by emergency crews on Tuesday.

Her father Hassan El-Khawas, 55, mother Zeina Alayn, 37, and 14-year-old sister Sara, died despite the efforts of paramedics at the scene.

Emergency services were called to the sea off Shoreham Fort at about 14:40 BST on Tuesday to a report of four people in difficulty in the water.

News.title: More students planning to live at home for university over 'insane' living costs
News.content:
More new students are choosing to live at home for university this year than at any point in the last nine years, new data shows.

Over 81,000 UK 18-year-olds said in their accepted university application that they intended to live at home this year, according to the Universities and Colleges Admissions Service (Ucas) - just over one in three students in that category.

In 2017, it was closer to one in five.

The figures vary across the UK - with 48% of applicants in Scotland intending to live at home, compared with 20% in Wales - but the trend is rising across the board.

Students told the BBC the rising cost of living was a major influence in deciding what to do after school or college.

For friends Beatrice and Amelia, who are from St Helens, Merseyside, the cost of accommodation was a big factor in their decision to live at home while studying.

Both are heading to university in September, but neither will be moving into student accommodation.

News.title: Burnham economic adviser O'Neill rules out government job
News.content:
The economist Lord Jim O'Neill, who has been advising the prime minister, has said he will not be taking a job in Andy Burnham's government.

Lord O'Neill, a crossbench peer, was once a treasury minister under the Conservatives.

As first reported by, external the Financial Times, he said he did not want the constraints involved in taking on a formal role.

The former chief economist at Goldman Sachs had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser.

He said he was enjoying what he was currently doing too much and did not want to have to give up control of his business interests to comply with official rules.

"I've decided to not take a formal role," he said.

"It's not because of any policy disagreements. I'm a massive fan of the focus on devolution and I hope Andy and his team will be bold on this and everything else."

"I'll continue to, hopefully, maintain an informal relationship with the PM and his team," he added.

He said he did not want "the constraints of a blind trust and all the constraints that would be necessary".

In placing shares in blind trusts, ministers have no knowledge of how their investment is being handled, to avoid any potential conflict of interest.

From 2015-2016, Lord O'Neill was commercial secretary to the Treasury under the then-Chancellor, George Osborne.

The peer, who grew up in Greater Manchester, was a key figure in pushing the Conservatives' Northern Powerhouse agenda, which was aimed at boosting the economy of the North of England.

Lord O'Neill is also known as the economist who coined the term Bric in 2001 to describe leading developing or newly industrialised countries with potential for fast growth and, therefore, investment returns.

The original four nations - Brazil, Russia, India and China - later became the Brics when they were joined by South Africa.

News.title: Meghan in talks for role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, BBC understands
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex is in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, the BBC has learned.

Discussions are in their early stages but this would be Meghan's first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

Much of the two previous series of The Gentlemen, which was created by Guy Ritchie, have been filmed in the Cotswolds - the area it is rumoured Harry and Meghan will set up home when they return to the UK later this month.

The Gentlemen, starring the actor Theo James, is a comedy series about a duke who becomes a drug baron.

The details of the discussions and any role Meghan might be offered have not yet been revealed.

Actors Hugh Bonneville and Vinnie Jones have appeared in previous series of the show.

Meghan was best known in acting for her part in the US legal drama, Suits, in which she played lawyer, Rachel Zane, for seven seasons. Her last episode aired in 2018.

News.title: How this 1960s ex-council house is managing to stay cool without air con
News.content:
After five heatwaves and plenty of advice on how to stay safe in what is set to become the UK's hottest summer on record, many people continue to find it a challenge to stay cool - particularly in their homes.

This is perhaps no surprise. More than half of homes, external in the UK are already at risk of overheating and at current rates of climate change this will rise to 92% by 2050 if we do not adapt.

But in south London, on a 35C day, one 1960s ex-council house with no air-conditioning is managing to beat the heat.

Marion Baeli's home is one of many across the UK being adapted for warmer - maybe even 40C - British summers.

News.title: As they return to the UK, Harry and Meghan search for a brand that sticks
News.content:
In late July, the Duchess of Sussex's lifestyle range, called As ever, launched a "rich, vibrant" blackberry spread alongside a softly lit video of her picking the fruit.

A month later, Meghan and her husband Prince Harry are returning to live in the UK just as blackberry season ends. Perhaps we can expect another video soon, shot on these shores.

Or perhaps not, because experts say the Harry and Meghan brand is at a crossroads.

After the Duke and Duchess of Sussex's acrimonious exit from the Royal Family in 2020, the projects marking their fresh start in California - from streaming to signature scents - have mostly failed to find large audiences, and experts say it's unclear where the couple goes from here.

Their return to the UK has surprised many and we don't know their reasons for the switch, but what's clear is that they will not be working royals when they return. So what could they be doing instead?

News.title: GTA 6 leaks - a nightmare or a blip for the biggest video game of the year?
News.content:
Video game journalist Wesley Yin-Poole, director of news at IGN, says the apparent leaks will be tough for the game's developers.

"GTA 6 is an enormous endeavour," says Yin-Poole. "It's being built over the course a decade, essentially, with thousands of people involved.

"To have the game exposed in this way will have been devastating to many people who worked on it."

The group behind the apparent leaks claims to be acting in the interests of players, accusing Rockstar of engaging in anti-consumer practices, such as its decision not to release a disc version of GTA 6 at launch.

Not everyone is convinced about the group's intentions, as each release of new material has invited viewers to send cryptocurrency "donations" to the user uploading them.

Stop Killing Games, which campaigns against all-digital distribution models, criticised the alleged leaks as "destructive" and urged people not to send money to those claiming responsibility.

Yin-Poole says there's "a huge amount of scepticism" about the stated motivation.

"Most people believe this is about money," he says, "it feels like, honestly, the whole 'we're doing this for the gamers' angle is nonsense, and I suspect most people have dismissed it."

So far, two official trailers for GTA 6 have been released, the most recent in May 2025. Since then, ardent fans have leapt on any rumours or apparent clues in official Rockstar posts.

Some famously came up with an elaborate theory, external suggesting an image of the moon included in a promotional post for GTA Online held clues to the release date of GTA 6's first trailer.

"To a certain extent, Rockstar has themselves to blame," says Vermeij. "That's their strategy - and I think it's a good strategy, it's exciting. But the consequence is that every little bit of information, every little event, gets sort of blown out of proportion."

Yin-Poole says while people will likely understand this isn't the way Rockstar had intended GTA6 to be revealed and doesn't show the game in the best light, he believes most will "reserve judgement" about it until they have seen official footage in action, or played it for themselves.

Ultimately, he believes there's little chance the leaks will "derail the potential success of the game".

"GTA 6 will be an unprecedented moment in pop culture history," he says. "So ultimately, this will become a footnote in the history of GTA 6's development."

Vermeij, who has not watched any of the latest leaks, agrees.

"I think it will have no impact at all whatsoever," he says. "People will have forgotten about it by the time the game comes out."

Grand Theft Auto 6 is due to be released on 19 November for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S, with a PC release expected at a later date.

News.title: Drugs at their fingertips, intense pressure: Why child stars fall into addiction
News.content:
Hayden Panettiere was 16 when drugs first arrived in her life in Hollywood.

Ahead of a red carpet event for the hit series Heroes, she has said someone on her team handed her a pill to help amp up her energy. The hit sci-fi NBC series had catapulted the teen into a household name - and that brought with it intense pressure and exhaustion she says felt overwhelming.

"Within minutes, a wave of energy washed over me, like I'd just woken up from the most refreshing night's sleep of my life," Panettiere wrote about that pill in her memoir, which was released just months before her death.

She called it "the gateway drug that ushered me toward the good of pharmaceuticals and the downfall of addiction".

The star's sudden death at the age of 36 has placed a renewed focus on her struggles with mental health and substance abuse, and re-ignited a discussion about the pressures of Hollywood on child stars.

The coroner's office in Greenville, South Carolina said crews treated a woman in "cardiac arrest" and her autopsy showed "no signs of trauma".

No cause of death has been released, though additional tests are yet to be completed.

Audio from police dispatchers and crews who responded to the address said they were responding to a "cardiac arrest" and detailed their efforts to resuscitate the woman after a possible "overdose". Panettiere's ex boyfriend, Brian Hickerson - who has admitted to abusing her - and his brother Zack, were with Panettiere when emergency services came, according to a police report.

There is no suggestion of wrongdoing on their part, according to police.

It is not known if drugs or alcohol played a factor in her death, but the US Drug Enforcement Agency is joining an investigation into her death, according to US media reports.

Panettiere is one of many actors who has openly struggled with addiction after exposure to fame at an early age, which addiction experts told the BBC can put people at risk for mental health and substance abuse issues.

It can sometimes seem to the rest of the world that child actors have "everything" at their fingertips - like fame and money, said Lucas Trautman, the medical director of Oxford Treatment Center, an addiction treatment centre in Mississippi.

"But it's important to remember that they were also exposed during a developmental time to many adult aspects of life that the rest of us weren't - including traumatic experiences - and so that gives them unique risk factors for addiction," Trautman said.

Panettiere's death comes after she published a memoir where she discussed at length her issues with addiction, her postpartum depression and the loss of her 28-year-old brother.

Panettiere's decision to publicly share her struggles is worthy of respect, said William Moyers, the vice-president of public affairs for Hazelden Betty Ford, the largest nonprofit addiction treatment provider in the US. But he said the constant public scrutiny she faced may not have allowed her room to address her mental health in private.

"Her entire life from the beginning was centred in the intense public spotlight, and this didn't give Hayden much in the way of a respite," said Moyers, who has been in recovery from an addiction since 1989.

News.title: Prince Harry and six others face privacy case legal bill of up to £34.5m
News.content:
Prince Harry and six other public figures face paying up to Â£34.5m to the publisher of the Daily Mail after a High Court judge imposed an exceptional order for legal costs over their failed privacy case.

The seven claimants, also including Sir Elton John and Liz Hurley, must pay an initial Â£9.54m by Friday of next week to Associated Newspapers Limited (ANL).

The judge ruled that the case was a rare one in which the claimants should have to pay far in excess of the costs that had been agreed before trial, criticising how they presented their claims as "unreasonable to a high degree".

On 7 July, Judge Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed the claims of unlawful information-gathering, which ANL denied.

The Duke of Sussex and the other six claimants have until 2 October to attempt to launch an appeal.

Those other claimants are Sir Elton John and his husband David Furnish, former Liberal Democrat deputy leader Sir Simon Hughes, racial justice campaigner Baroness Lawrence, and actresses Sadie Frost and Liz Hurley,

They had insurance to cover up to Â£16.2m of Association Newspapers' costs in the event of losing the case - but Friday's ruling means the newspaper group could now try to recover up to the Â£34.5m that it said it had to spend to defend itself. This means the duke and others could face a bill of some Â£18m.

Justice Nicklin said: "I regard a claim for costs in excess of Â£34 million as, on its face, excessive and as giving rise to real concerns as to whether all of the costs now claimed by Associated were reasonably incurred and are reasonable in amount."

But he added he had "decided not to impose a ceiling on Associated's recoverable costs", as it would "be too broad-brushed, would risk unfairness, and would be vulnerable to the charge that it was arbitrary".

The judge also ruled that ANL's costs should be determined on an indemnity basis, which is more favourable to the publisher in terms of the amount it can recover, aside from where orders had already been made.

He added it was "striking" that "not a single allegation of serious wrongdoing was voluntarily withdrawn" by the group of seven claimants.

He said: "That matters. Serious allegations of criminality or grave impropriety cannot properly be left hanging over individuals in that way.

"If a party no longer advances such an allegation, or no longer has a proper evidential basis for advancing it, the allegation should be withdrawn clearly and in terms.

News.title: Brief break from rain as sunshine returns for weekend
News.content:
After the spell of showery weather earlier this week, a strong area of high pressure is set to bring bright and sunny weather to much of the UK this weekend.

Daytime temperatures will feel pleasantly warm - though a long way off from the record heat experienced earlier this month.

Nights are expected to be mostly clear, leading to a significant temperature contrast from morning lows to afternoon highs.

While Saturday and Sunday will bring a brief break from the rain for many, unsettled weather will return early next week.

News.title: Murder probe after wildfire uncovers body in park
News.content:
A murder investigation is under way after human bones were uncovered at a west London park following a wildfire, the Metropolitan Police said.

Emergency services were called to Bedfont Lakes Country Park in Hounslow at about 18:35 BST on Wednesday, 12 August.

A police spokesperson said the remains were found by a member of the public after the wildfire affected an area of woodland known as The Pits.

Following a post-mortem examination, police said the bones belonged to a woman aged between 25 and 45. They said it was not clear how long the remains had been there and officers were still working to identify her.

News.title: Arran ferry evacuated over 'bomb threat' by passenger rescued from sea
News.content:
A 23-year-old man has been arrested after a ferry service on Scotland's west coast was evacuated over a bomb threat.

Operator CalMac said a passenger was reported overboard on the MV Caledonian Isles 16:40 service, carrying 329 people from Brodick on the Isle of Arran.

The BBC understands that after being pulled from the sea by the ferry's rescue boat, the man then told crew that there was a bomb on board.

All passengers were removed on foot at Ardrossan so the vessel could be searched. Police Scotland said it was established that the threats "were not credible".

The passengers and others waiting at the port were taken to a nearby supermarket car park by police while the search was carried out.

After this was complete, officers allowed people back on board to collect their vehicles.

News.title: Ofcom investigating Sky News over Farage harassment claims
News.content:
Ofcom would not comment on any investigation but said it treated complaints in strict confidence and would not "publicly confirm the identities of individuals concerned".

Farage claims reporters from Sky News approached his daughter's home while he was out of the country.

Sky News says it did not interact with his daughter, and was trying to ask Farage about a Â£5m gift he received from cryptocurrency investor Christopher Harborne before he entered Parliament in July 2024.

A parliamentary standards investigation into whether the gift broke any rules resumed earlier this month after Farage was re-elected as MP for Clacton following a by-election he triggered that was boycotted by the other major parties.

Upon returning to the country, Farage was questioned by Sky News over the undeclared gift, to which he responded: "You tell your bosses, you harass my family any more, there will be serious consequences, that's what your organisation has done this morning, now go away."

When pressed on the donation again, he said: "Did you not hear me? You have broken all the rules, Leveson and everything else, cut."

At the time, Sky News said in a post on X: "Sky News was not at the property at 7.41am. As has already been acknowledged, and as shown in the footage from 10.19am, Sky News was outside a property where Mr Farage was registered to vote at the last election.

"Sky News did not interact with Mr Farage's daughter.

"On a single occasion, we approached the property without a camera operator, identified ourselves as Sky News and the adult occupant chose not to engage. We were seeking to contact Mr Farage to ask questions about the gift he accepted from Mr Cottrell.

"This is a well-established and routine journalistic practice when reporting on matters of legitimate public interest.

"The footage clearly demonstrates that Sky News did not 'hound' or pursue Mr Farage's daughter.

"At no stage did we seek to speak to anyone other than Mr Farage in connection with this story."

The BBC has contacted Sky News for comment.

Ofcom says it aims to conclude fairness and privacy complaints within 90 working days.

News.title: Under-fives and pregnant women told to avoid runny eggs when eating out over salmonella risk
News.content:
Vulnerable people are being warned not to eat under-cooked or runny eggs when they are eating out because of the developing salmonella outbreak.

The Food Standards Agency (FSA) told the BBC the under fives, over 65s, women who are pregnant and those with health conditions should avoid them along with freshly-made products that might contain uncooked eggs, such as mayonnaise, souffle and hollandaise sauce.

But the FSA said well-cooked eggs in restaurants, cafes and from takeaways were fine to eat.

It comes after the UK Health Security Agency declared a national outbreak of salmonella food poisoning after one person died and hundreds more fell ill.

It is thought imported eggs or dishes containing them are behind the outbreak.

FSA chief scientific adviser Ian Young said: "If people are eating out or consuming eggs or egg-containing products from cafes and restaurants then for those people in particular who are young, elderly, pregnant or vulnerable, it's important to make sure that any eggs or egg products that you consume in those settings have been very well cooked."

He described the outbreak as "unusually large and rapidly increasing", and added that "people need to be careful".

But he reiterated the message that it was fine for people to buy British eggs from supermarkets as chickens bred here are vaccinated against common strains of salmonella.

"There is no link to those eggs to this current outbreak," he added.

Mark Williams, chief executive of the British Egg Industry Council, said eggs from Britain were safe to eat when runny, even for vulnerable people, and were widely available in restaurants and cafÃ©s.

"Customers who want to enjoy a runny egg should simply ask whether British Lion eggs are being used," he said.

News.title: Men admit trying to tunnel into jewellery shop
News.content:
Three men who were caught trying to tunnel into a jewellery shop from a neighbouring massage parlour have admitted conspiracy to commit burglary.

Ioan Asafeti, 39, Laurentiu-Daniel Nitisoara, 38, both of no fixed address, and Sergiu Plastin, 42, of Portadown, County Armagh, were behind the attempted raid on Mitcham Road in Tooting, south London, in the early hours of 17 July.

Kingston Crown Court heard how body-worn camera footage captured Nitisoara being arrested in a nearby alleyway, while Asafeti was found hiding on a rooftop.

Plastin was tracked down using mobile phone data and arrested later that day at Stansted Airport as he tried to board a flight to Ireland.

News.title: Man denies charge over Manchester synagogue attack
News.content:
A man has denied failing to disclose information in relation to the Manchester synagogue attack.

Hekmat Omar Ali Hakim appeared before Westminster Magistrates' Court and pleaded not guilty to failing to disclose information regarding terrorist activity.

The 49-year-old, of St James Road in Higher Broughton, Salford, spoke only to confirm his name and indicate his plea. He was remanded into custody to appear at at the Old Bailey on 25 September.

Worshippers Melvin Cravitz and Adrian Daulby were killed when Jihad Al-Shamie, 35, a Syrian-born British citizen, drove into the gates of the Heaton Park Hebrew Congregation Synagogue on 2 October.

He then began attacking with a knife, while wearing a fake suicide belt, before being shot dead by police outside the synagogue.

Between morning feedings, the gibbons break into loud song.

Their vocalizations — ranging from screeching and siren-like calls to guttural hoots and low grunts — echo across a sanctuary in the dry, hot hills of the Santa Clarita Valley, just north of Los Angeles.

Over the last 50 years, the Gibbon Conservation Center has grown from housing a modest assortment of animals into a globally recognized facility dedicated exclusively to gibbon welfare and care. Famed for their distinctive vocal calls, they are among the world's rarest and most critically endangered primates.

Currently, the facility cares for approximately 40 gibbons from five distinct species. Their singing can occasionally be heard up to a mile away by the few residents living on the sparsely populated outskirts of Santa Clarita.

The sanctuary was established by the late Alan Mootnick, a self-taught primatologist who became a prominent authority on gibbons while simultaneously operating a home painting and remodelling business.

He published research papers in academic journals, welcomed international researchers, and answered queries from fellow scientists regarding gibbon identification and care.

open image in gallery A gibbon peers through the fence of an enclosure at the Gibbon Conservation Center in Santa Clarita, CA ( AP )

“Sometimes they would just send him a picture of a rescued gibbon asking what species, or they will play him a vocalization,” director Gabi Skollar said.

Skollar moved from Hungary to the U.S. in 2005 to learn from Mootnick and work at the center. She has carried on his mission since his sudden death from heart surgery complications in 2011.

Skollar, who had initially planned to leave the job to continue her education, said that she could not abandon the gibbons.

“We have to keep going and take care of this place,” she said.

Now, she lives on-site with another caretaker, waking up every morning to the cacophony of gibbons at sunrise. They are her children, she said.

Each gibbon has their own quirks

open image in gallery Gibbon Conservation Center director Gabi Skollar feeds one of the little apes ( AP )

Having spent decades at the conservation centre, Skollar is intimately familiar with the distinct personalities of the gibbons residing there.

A young northern white-cheeked gibbon named Pepper regularly prompts the group to begin their singing sessions, which are brought to a close by a pileated gibbon named Violet and her partner Truman. Meanwhile, Pierre, a rescued gibbon, harbors a dislike of men.

The small apes vocalize three to four times every day, singing for 20 to 30 minutes at a time.

Skollar, who is researching gibbon vocalization for a doctorate at the University of California, Los Angeles, said: “There’s a lot of things that we can learn in a captive setting that can be shared with conservationists in the field and also with people working in sanctuaries rescuing gibbons.”

The primates face rising threats in their natural Southeast Asian tropical rainforest habitats, where deforestation continues to destroy their environment. The illicit wildlife trade poses a severe risk, as young gibbons are routinely taken from their parents to be sold as pets. Wild populations for some of the species cared for at the centre have dwindled to fewer than 2,000 apes.

Mootnick bought his first gibbon, Spanky, in 1976 after responding to a newspaper advert. Today, the population is maintained both through births at the site and exchanges with other facilities to safeguard genetic diversity in breeding programmes.

open image in gallery Two gibbons eat in an enclosure at the Gibbon Conservation Center ( AP )

The center became the first to successfully breed the endangered Javan gibbon, a species native exclusively to Java in Indonesia, and is preparing to send a pair of northern white-cheeked gibbons to the Pittsburgh Zoo.

Caretakers connect with apes

On a recent morning, on-site caretaker Jodi Kleier was making the rounds with buckets of washed lettuce, steamed sweet potatoes and bananas. She handed a young gibbon, Rocky, a piece of chopped banana as he reached out through the fence.

Rocky was hand-reared by Kleier after being abandoned by his mother after birth at the center, which can happen with first-time mothers if they went through a difficult birth.

Kleier has worked at the center for a decade, and started out as a volunteer. She has a tattoo of Rocky on her thigh.

She fell in love with gibbons after coming to the center for a primatology course in school.

open image in gallery On-site caretaker Jodi Kleier hands a piece of banana to a gibbon ( AP )

“I love watching any primates play, because I think they’re so natural to us, we kind of see ourselves in them,” she said.

Kleier and volunteers who come by during the week are constantly washing and cooking produce because they feed the gibbons five to six times a day to imitate the pace of their foraging behavior in the wild.

“The Javans, they’re my favorite species and the male Javan is singing … one of my favorite songs,” Kleier said of a ghostly vocalization. “In Javanese folklore, they’re known as these spirits that live in the forest because you can always hear them.”

Schools and tourists can visit

While the center is only open to visitors for guided tours on the weekends, they receive steady interest from schools, tourists and senior centers.

They also work with local organizations such as The Teaching Zoo at Moorpark College to help students receive hands-on experience in animal care. The college takes first-year students on a field trip to the Gibbon Conservation Center every year, and many have gone on to work there after they graduate.

“When I went out there for the first time in the 1990s, I didn’t know what a gibbon was,” said Mara Rodriguez, a development coordinator who's been with the zoo for decades. “Now I’ve raised four gibbons in my career.”

Anyone who visits “will leave with a lasting impression and begin to care about the species,” she said.

Skollar’s long-term goal is to raise more money to build larger enclosures for the gibbons and construct an education center for visitors. She hopes to continue honoring Mootnick’s legacy and dedicating her life to the gibbons — one of which is named after him.

“When he passed away, I just felt that he’s around and helping us keep this center going,” she said.

As I sit in my home in Swabi, in Pakistan’s Gandhara region, nestled between two mighty rivers, the Indus and Kabul, I’ve been unable to tear myself away from the images of yellow, dried land across England. Pictures of the once-green historic Greenwich park in London, where I first studied years ago, now looks like a dusty wasteland.

The chaos of the climate crisis, bringing extreme heat, droughts and floods, has been on Pakistan’s doorstep for some time now, but it’s clear the world is now catching up to a reality it can no longer ignore.

And this year, we face the double threat of the climate crisis and an unprecedented 'super' El Niño, all against the background of global aid cuts and ever dwindling international climate finance budgets.

El Nino – which begins with above-average warming in the Pacific and results in disruption to weather patterns around the world – is a normal climatic phenomenon. However, as our global temperatures increase through climate change, it's even more challenging for countries to prepare, plan, and adapt for when El Niño hits.

Clearly, this is not the time for world leaders to be walking back their climate commitments.

New research from WaterAid and the Universities of Bristol and Cardiff shows how El Niño is likely to disrupt or intensify rainfall patterns in some of the world’s biggest cities across Asia an East Africa. In cities like Phnom Penh (Cambodia), a strong El Niño can bring unusually low rainfall for the typically flood-prone region, and with it the threat of drought; meanwhile cities like Colombo (Sri Lanka), could see significantly higher rainfall, raising the risk of flooding and major urban disruption.

For my own Pakistan, cities like Faisalabad and Karachi are curiously situated in a "transition zone" of El Niño, where both higher and lower rainfall could occur, the data finds. Practically, this means El Niño is bringing even more climate uncertainty, making the coming months extremely challenging for governments to prepare for.

Yet, as a country on the frontline of the climate crisis, we are accustomed to this insecurity. Water stressed countries like my own have had no choice but to find solutions to our chaotic new climate – often pioneering approaches that the rest of the world can learn from.

open image in gallery Commuters wade through a flooded street after heavy rainfall in Rawalpindi, Pakistan ( AFP/Getty )

One method which can act as a critical lifeline is rainwater harvesting and artificial groundwater recharge; systems which collect and divert rainwater before cleaning & storing it for future use. This can be used to replenish depleted underwater reserves, while reducing pressure on freshwater supplies.

This simple but effective system works across Pakistan’s diverse landscapes: capturing 400,000 gallons of water each year in Karachi, in a coastal megacity facing water shortages and urban flooding. In Islamabad, WaterAid Pakistan and its partners developed a water recharge site at Kachnar Park.

Since 2022, it has recharged nearly 40 million gallons of water – equivalent to more than 18 Olympic size swimming pools every year – and contributed to an almost 5 metre rise in the local groundwater levels. This isn't a small-scale solution. It's the future.

Just before the monsoon of 2026, Islamabad passed new legislation making rainwater harvesting mandatory for new buildings, in a step which will have transformative impacts on future water security.

This will be a game-changer for Pakistan, helping communities capture rain, replenish rapidly declining groundwater and build a more secure water supply for generations to come.

As aid budgets come under pressure globally, these are exactly the kinds of proven water solutions that overseas finance and climate funding should prioritise, backed by local expertise and delivered through long-term partnerships.

As we all wake up to this new era of climate instability and start to truly comprehend the consequences on our water security, perhaps it's worth taking note of the solutions pioneered by countries who've had no other choice but to adapt to survive.

London is no stranger to rain. After England’s fifth heatwave of the year, I wonder how different Greenwich Park would look during this hot, dry, summer, if we'd learn lessons from countries like my own.

I hope – and urge – world leaders to use this summer as a lesson in the importance of climate adaptation, and preparation ahead of the upcoming El Niño. Now we have the data to predict the impact, and the solutions to cope. Next, we need the investment – before the next storm inevitably arrives.

Dr Shakeel Hayat is a climate change & WASH (Water, Sanitation and Hygiene) specialist at WaterAid Pakistan

At least two people were killed overnight in Ukraine by Russian drone and missile strikes, authorities said, a day after an attack on a shopping center killed 16 people.

Oleksandr Pertsovsky, the head of Ukraine’s national rail operator Ukrzaliznytsia, said Saturday that one of the company’s employees was killed in an overnight ballistic missile attack on the railway in the capital Kyiv.

Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Saturday its forces had hit a locomotive depot.

Moscow’s forces have recently intensified their ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, exploiting Ukraine’s chronic shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, the sole weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down the missiles.

Russian drone strikes also killed one person overnight in Zaporizhzhia, local officials said Saturday.

The latest attacks came a day after Russian drones struck a shopping center in the city of Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine on Friday.

Dnipropetrovsk regional head Oleksandr Hanzha said in the early hours of Saturday that the death toll had risen to 16 and nine people remain missing after the attack, which wounded another 130.

Kryvyi Rih is the hometown of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who described the attack as a double-tap strike, in which an initial wave of drones hit the area followed by a second wave as rescue workers responded.

Kryvyi Rih has been hit multiple times during the more than 4-year-old war, with one of the deadliest occurring in April 2025, when 20 people were killed, including nine children.

Large-scale Russian strikes have become a regular occurrence this summer, with Friday’s attacks landing just 24 hours after Russia pounded Kyiv with scores of missiles and drones in a nighttime assault that killed 16 people.

The capital has been hit hard repeatedly in recent weeks: 17 people were killed in a strike on Kyiv and its surrounding region just over two weeks ago, and nine died in another attack on the city two days before that. The United Nations said last week that Kyiv was one of the hardest-hit cities in July, with at least 54 civilians killed and 202 injured.

At the same time, Ukraine has shifted the war onto Russian soil through long-range drone strikes on oil facilities that have caused fuel shortages across the country. It also has unsettled the Russian public by striking warehouses of Wildberries, the country’s biggest online retailer.

This year’s El Niño weather event could be the “strongest in a lifetime,” weather experts have warned

That's due to unusually warm sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean. This natural climate pattern occurs when east-to-west trade winds weaken, allowing warm water to shift eastward.

This is what fuels more storms and clouds over the region that can cause ripple effects through the global atmosphere - and the U.S. is no exception.

But AccuWeather Lead Long-Range Meteorologist Paul Pastelok said whether this El Niño breaks records or not, "it is about the impacts and the impacts will not change either way.”

open image in gallery The 2026-2027 El Niño climate pattern is expected to be very strong and potentially the strongest ‘in a lifetime,’ forecasters warn. That could mean more extreme weather impacts across America ( Getty Images )

The El Niño is already impacting weather in the U.S., stymying this year’s Atlantic hurricane production.

Expected to last through next year, the pattern should bring lingering heat through the fall months in northern and eastern states.

And it’s projected to send drenching storms across the southern swath of the country while the Atlantic stays quiet.

During the winter, El Niño could bring snow, sleet and freezing rain to the Southeast and southern Plains.

And Florida could see more thunderstorms than usual, while other parts of the Gulf Coast see less, according to CNN meteorologist Mary Gilbert.

Unfortunately, after the worst spring drought on record, any resulting snowpack is anticipated to provide little relief for the West’s decades-long water crisis.

“Even one big year is not going to save us,” John Berggren, a policy manager at environmental nonprofit Western Resource Advocates, told WIRED. “It might be a sigh of relief, but we'll be right back in it.”

Next year’s forecast is murkier, but temperatures could soar, and federal forecasters said last week that there is a 90 percent chance the 2026-2027 El Niño will reach the highest strength level.

There are four different strength levels, ranging from “weak” to “very strong.”

El Niño is the warm phase of the climate pattern known as the El Niño Southern Oscillation, which regulates global climate. These events occur every 2-7 years.

open image in gallery The El Nino pattern is the warm phase of the climate pattern known as the El Nino Southern Oscillation. It brings wetter weather in the southern states and warmer and drier conditions up north ( NOAA )

The last time the El Niño was this strong was in 1877, when a global famine killed more than 50 million people.

“Simultaneous multiyear droughts similar to those in the 1870s could happen again,” Deepti Singh, an associate professor at Washington State University, told The Washington Post in May.

“What is different now is that our atmosphere and oceans are substantially warmer than they were in the 1870s, which means the associated extremes could be more extreme,” she said.

How much human-caused climate change plays a role here is an ongoing debate.

But it’s clear that there are higher temperatures and stronger storms now due to climate change. This past July was the warmest on record.

“What we’ll see in 2027 is a sneak peek of what the new normal will be in 2035,” Zeke Hausfather, a climate scientist at Berkeley Earth, a nonprofit research organization, told The New York Times. “We’ll see things that have never happened before in our history in terms of temperature, drought conditions, extreme heat.”
