World.title: Abike Ilu: ‘My drum hairstyle is my identity and mission to preserve Yoruba culture’
World.content:
By Ishola Balogun

She is impossible to miss in a crowd. Cultural entertainer and drummer Abike Ilu has a unique hairstyle in the image of a talking drum which has become her signature hairstyle. For Abike, the look is not just about style. It is a statement of identity and a mission to keep Yoruba heritage alive.

“The drum-inspired hairstyle is more than a fashion statement; it is my identity and a symbol of my passion for Yoruba culture,” she said in a chat.

“As a talking drummer, I wanted something that immediately tells people who I am and what I represent before I even perform. Maintaining it requires time, commitment, and resources, but I see it as an investment in my brand. It has sparked conversations, made me easily recognizable, and helped people remember me wherever I go. Many now identify me simply by that unique look. So yes, it has achieved its purpose.

Abike Ilu describes herself as a cultural entertainer, talking drummer, and performer whose core mission is to preserve and promote Yoruba heritage through music and stagecraft. Her sound, she explains, is a fusion of ancestral rhythms and contemporary presentation.

“My style blends traditional talking drum rhythms with contemporary sounds and modern stage presentation. This allows me to connect with older audiences who appreciate tradition and younger generations who enjoy modern entertainment. I believe culture should evolve without losing its originality, and that is exactly what my music represents. It is Afro-cultural”, she said.

The drummer has been busy on the circuit in recent months. Her performances have spanned cultural festivals, weddings, corporate events, community celebrations, and social gatherings. She has also leveraged online platforms and media content to reach audiences beyond live shows.

For Abike, each drumbeat is both entertainment and advocacy, a way to ensure that Yoruba tradition remains visible, relevant and exciting for new generations. In an industry where young talents often struggle for recognition, Abike Ilu has chosen a path where culture is the brand, the drum is the voice, and heritage is the message.

World.title: 3.5m missing births:: How hospitals can close Nigeria’s registration gap
World.content:
… Experts add: Register them where they are born

By Chioma Obinna

The first cry came, then the rush of hands. A newborn baby girl had just entered the world. While nurses attended to the mother and cleaned the baby, Emmanuel Joseph was already thinking beyond the excitement of fatherhood.



He wanted his daughter to exist not only in his family, but also in the records of the country.

Within minutes of his wife’s delivery, Joseph walked out of the labour area in search of the nurse in charge.



“I asked if they had a desk where I could register the birth of my child,” he told Good health weekly.

The nurse was surprised.



“She asked if I really had a name for my child because the child would not be registered if I did not have a name. I told her yes.”



Joseph was directed to a National Population Commission, NPC, registration unit within the hospital.

There, another surprise awaited the registrar.



“They were also surprised that I came for a child that the nurses were still busy cleaning up,” he said.

But the registrar quickly got to work. A chair was provided, a form brought out and Joseph completed the necessary details.

His daughter was registered. Free of charge.

Before the family left the hospital, Joseph had in his hands what could become one of the most important documents in his daughter’s life — her birth certificate.

“I know the importance of birth registration and what it means for a child. It shows that the child is a Nigerian and can be budgeted for and counted. She will need it all through her life,” he said.

For Joseph, the experience was simple. For millions of Nigerian children, however, getting that first legal identity remains anything but simple.

Across Lagos, Ogun, Oyo, Osun, Ondo, Ekiti and Edo states, an estimated 3.5 million children are without birth certificates, according to officials reports. These children are not missing and not necessarily abandoned.

But they are living in homes, going to hospitals, attending clinics and growing up within communities but whose births may never have been entered into the official records of the country.

In the words of Chief of UNICEF Lagos Field Office, Celine Lafoucriere: “They are children who are alive, at home, loved by their families, but completely invisible to their state and the country.

“Some are in cities. Some are in villages. Some were born in hospitals and still never got registered. The gap is everywhere.”

The contradiction is stark.

A child may be born inside a health facility, surrounded by doctors, nurses, midwives and health workers, yet leave that same facility without a legal identity. That is the gap health facilities could help close.

The delivery room as the first registration point. Hospitals, maternity centres and primary healthcare facilities occupy a unique position in the life of a newborn.

They know when a baby is born. They know where the child was born. They have access to the mother, father or caregiver at one of the few moments when the entire family is physically present. They are therefore potentially the most strategic entry points for universal birth registration.

According to experts, there was need to make birth registration part of routine maternal and newborn care, just as immunisation, weighing, postnatal checks and other essential services are integrated into the continuum of care.

The civil registration system itself recognises this opportunity.

One of the key accelerators identified for scaling up legal identity services is the integration of birth registration with primary healthcare services, alongside decentralisation, digitalisation, data interoperability and social mobilisation. The strategy envisages birth registration becoming an integral component of PHC services and expanding registration points to wards and health facilities.

The logic is compelling.

Instead of asking a mother who has just delivered a baby to make another journey to a distant registration centre, the registration service comes to the place where the birth has already been recorded.

Instead of relying on parents to know that registration is free, health workers can tell them.

Instead of waiting weeks or months, registration can begin before the mother leaves the facility.

And instead of treating birth registration as a bureaucratic afterthought, it becomes part of protecting the child from the moment of birth.

A mother’s experience

Duke Juliet, a mother of two, understands the value of that document. “I just wanted to do a birth certificate for my child. Because I know that it’s very important,” she said.

Her experience was largely seamless.

She filled the form, submitted it and received the certificate without paying.

When she later returned for immunisation, she was informed that the document was ready.

Her experience with her first child was less straightforward. At one point, she had to redo the registration because the handwritten document was not ready for printing.

The newer process, she said, was faster.

“This one didn’t take up to a month. This one came out. There was no money,” she said.

For Juliet, the lesson for other mothers is clear: information must follow women into the health system.

“For other women, I think that once they go for immunization and all, they will be informed.”

For Juliet, every antenatal clinic, every delivery room, every postnatal clinic, every immunisation session and every PHC visit could become an opportunity to ask one simple question: “Has this child been registered?”

Where the system works, and where it breaks

At on of the Primary Healthcare in Sangotedo, area of Lagos, the transition from paper to digital birth registration is already exposing both the promise and the weaknesses of the new system.

According to Mr. Gabriel Aboton-Philip, NPC Registrar-in-Charge of Sangotedo, paper registration was officially discontinued from July 1, 2026, with registration moving online.

The digital system, he said, has been welcomed by more educated parents.

But for families in surrounding communities, the transition has exposed another layer of exclusion.

The first obstacle is the National Identification Number, NIN.

“Many of the mothers or the fathers don’t have NIN,” Aboton-Philip said.

He recalled spending four days at the registration point for a free online registration exercise for children aged zero to five.

Seventy-six people submitted their details.

Only 46 were successfully registered.

In some cases, parents provided NINs but their information could not be retrieved on the system.

Then comes another familiar problem, connectivity.

“When we register sometimes, when it gets to the point of submitting, sometimes it delays,” he said.

The problem, he explained, is internet connectivity.

The registrar therefore developed a workaround. Instead of keeping mothers waiting indefinitely, his team collects their details on a form and contacts them when necessary.

“With good network, within five minutes, you are done with your registration. But if there are network challenges, sometimes it takes as long as 10 to 15 minutes, dealing with one person,” he said.

The lesson is uncomfortable but important.

Digitalisation can make birth registration faster, cheaper and more accessible.

But digitalisation without reliable connectivity, functioning identity databases and trained personnel can simply move the barriers from a paper desk to a computer screen.

Invisible barriers

For families who fail to register their children, the reasons are not always neglect. Sometimes it is distance. Sometimes money. Sometimes language. Sometimes ignorance. Sometimes a lack of registration centres. Sometimes a parent does not understand why the document matters until the child urgently needs it.

Speaking at a birth registration media dialogue in Lagos, the UNICEF Child Protection Specialist, Mr. Denise Onoise, identified limited accessibility, inadequate registration centres, long distances, language barriers, inefficient registration processes and insufficient financial, human and material resources as major obstacles.

He noted that the burden is not only the official cost of registration.

Families may also spend money travelling to registration points, lose income by taking time away from work, make repeated journeys and endure poor-quality services.

“The problem is compounded in hard-to-reach areas and among disadvantaged population groups,” he said.

This is why the hospital could be more than a place where a child is delivered.

It could be the first gateway to citizenship. The price of being invisible. A birth certificate is often dismissed as a piece of paper that can be obtained later. But that paper represents much more. It establishes a child’s legal identity, name, gender, place and date of birth and provides information governments need for planning health, education, housing and social protection programmes.

For UNICEF’s Lafoucriere: “A birth certificate is not a piece of paper. It is a child’s ticket into school. It is what allows a doctor to put a name on a patient file. It is how a family proves their child is theirs.”

Without it, she warned, a child may face difficulties proving identity later in life, including accessing passports, voting and inheritance.

The consequences can become even more dangerous for vulnerable children.

Further, Onoise in his presentation, further identified risks ranging from exclusion from education, healthcare, social protection and justice systems to child marriage, child labour, trafficking, abuse, exploitation and family separation.

Children in marginalised, underserved and hard-to-reach communities are particularly exposed.

In other words, failure to register a birth does not merely create an administrative inconvenience.

It can create a lifetime of vulnerability.

NIN hurdle

Nigeria’s move towards digital birth registration is also bringing the country’s identity systems face-to-face with one another.

The current system requires parents to provide NIN details, while the birth registration process is designed to link the child to the national identity framework.

Registrars told parents that registration for children aged zero to five is free and that parents should ensure their NIN information is correct before registration.

The registrar also explained that the child must be physically present for capturing and that the system generates a NIN for the child.

That integration could eventually create a seamless identity chain from birth to adulthood.

But the Sangotedo experience shows why the chain must be as strong as its weakest link.

If a mother does not have a NIN, the child’s registration may stall.

If the NIN database does not return the parent’s details, registration may stall. If the internet fails, registration may stall. If there are too few registrars, registration may stall.

And if the family lives far from a registration point, they may never start.

The answer, therefore, is not simply to digitise. It is to bring the entire system closer to families.

Experts say a registration desk beside the weighing scale would bridge gaps and ensures infants are given immediate legal identity.

The case for integration with healthcare is already contained in the reform agenda.

The proposed approach includes decentralising services to local governments and establishing more registration points at ward and health-facility levels. It also calls for stronger interoperability between civil registration, health and identity management systems.

Imagine a mother arriving at a PHC for her baby’s immunisation.

The nurse checks the child’s vaccination card. The health worker asks whether the birth has been registered.

If not, the mother is immediately referred to an NPC registrar stationed within the facility or connected digitally to the registration system.

The registrar verifies the parents’ details. The baby is captured.

The birth is registered.

The NIN is generated.

The certificate is issued.

One visit. One integrated system.

One less child invisible to government. That is the promise.

But the reality remains unfinished.

However, according to Onoise on lessons learned from civil registration efforts showed that community-based registration expanded coverage and helped identify previously unregistered children. Digital registration improved efficiency and data quality, while interoperability strengthened coordination.

He further revealed major weaknesses such as health-facility interoperability had stalled at the profiling stage, with none of 371 targeted facilities live despite completed training. The birth notification pipeline had recorded zero notifications in the reporting year, while certificate issuance lagged behind registration — 120,469 certificates issued against 443,162 registrations.

That is the unfinished business.

The delivery room is ready.

The technology is emerging.

The parents are already there.

What is missing is a system capable of connecting all three.

From paper to a national identity

Nigeria’s civil registration architecture remains fragmented, with different agencies collecting identity-related information for different purposes.

The National Identity Management Commission manages NIN; NPC handles population and civil registration data; immigration manages passports; the Federal Road Safety Corps manages driver’s licences; the Central Bank of Nigeria manages BVN, while INEC handles voter registration, among others.

The fragmentation means critical child-related services such as school enrolment, immunisation and child justice do not yet operate through one unified identity system linked to birth registration.

The Partnership Compact involving NPC, the Association of Local Governments of Nigeria, NIMC, UNICEF and Barnksforte Technologies Limited is designed to tackle some of these weaknesses through harmonisation, decentralisation, stronger infrastructure and universal access.

Under the proposed arrangement, NPC would manage the national birth and death registration system and work with local governments; ALGON would support implementation at local level and establish additional registration centres; NIMC would ensure identity-system integration and prompt NIN assignment; while UNICEF would provide technical, financial and technological support.

The ambition is bigger than issuing certificates.

It is about building a child-centred identity system that follows a Nigerian from birth through the services and opportunities that define life.

A child born today should not have to become an adult before the country can prove that the child exists.

The health system can change that.

The first opportunity may come within minutes of birth.

Joseph’s daughter is proof that when the system is available, when the parent understands its value and when the registrar is within reach, registration can happen before the family even leaves the hospital.

His story should not be an exception.

It should be the standard.

Because every newborn arrives with more than a name chosen by parents.

Every child arrives with a right to identity. And perhaps the most powerful place to begin protecting that right is where life itself begins — in the delivery room.

The challenge now is to ensure that no mother walks out of a Nigerian hospital holding her newborn, while the country has yet to record that the child was ever born.

Explaining how the e- birth registration works, the Lagos State Director of the National Population Commission, Sherifdeen Kekere-Ekun Mr Kekere-Ekun emphasized that birth registration is now fully free for children between 0 to 5 years.

“We are no longer doing that handwritten registration. It has been phased out. We are now using digitalized one. This is digitalized birth certificate for your child.

0 to 5 years old is free. When you want to register your child, you must come with your NIN.

Your NIN or your husband’s NIN. And make sure that the name is correct. The name on the NIN and the name that is going to be on the child’s birth certificate is correct.

All the information, you have to give it to the registrar in charge to register your child. You are not paying 0 to 5 years. So once your child is above 5 years and you didn’t register, it’s called late registration.

That is when you have to make payment. And the payment is N5,000. And you must provide an email to be able to log in.

The old one is still valid. If you have registered the old one before 1st July, 2026, it’s still valid. You can still make use of it. But that’s not what we call it. We issue that manual only.”

“For mothers, if you don’t want to change your name for your parents’ name and you want to still maintain your father’s name, it’s still okay. So whatever name that you have on your NIN is what is going to be applicable, to be applied on this birth certificate.

So once there is a mistake on your NIN, you have to correct it before coming to the birth registration office. But if you want to change your husband’s name, there’s no problem. You have to make that correction before coming to the birth certificate office. Normally it takes 3 days. That is 72 hours. So that the NIN of your child will be applied.”

“It also has a tracking eye that you can see here. You have to bring your baby when coming to register. You must come with your baby for capturing. Pictures are not acceptable when you are coming to register the baby.”

Explaining some of the hitches, he said the NIN could not be confirmed or unable to submit, it may delay registration.

He charged the media to move beyond reporting statistics and government activities by taking the birth registration message directly to parents and caregivers in communities.

He stressed that accurate registration of births was also essential for effective governance, as reliable demographic data would enable government to determine the number and distribution of children and plan adequately for education, healthcare, social protection and other services.

World.title: Gunmen invade Mosques, abduct worshippers in Niger
World.content:
By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo

MINNA — Gunmen have reportedly invaded several communities in Borgu Local Government Area of Niger State, abducting an unspecified number of worshippers shortly after Friday prayers.

The attacks reportedly occurred in Dekara, Gidan Zana, Sabon Gida and Masaka communities, according to residents and the federal lawmaker representing the area, Hon. Jafar Muhammad Shetiman Borgu.

Shetiman Borgu, who confirmed the attacks to the BBC, monitored by our correspondent, said the actual number of people abducted had yet to be ascertained.

He said several worshippers were attacked with machetes, while some managed to escape with injuries.

“Some people managed to escape, while others sustained machete wounds,” he was quoted as saying.

According to him, the attackers entered Dekara after Friday prayers, surrounded a mosque and took worshippers into the forest.

He added that the gunmen subsequently moved into neighbouring communities, where they abducted more people after Friday prayers.

The lawmaker said youths and heads of households were among those taken away.

The latest attacks have heightened concerns over the security situation in Borgu, which borders Kebbi and Kwara states as well as the Republic of Benin.

Shetiman Borgu said forests in the area had become hideouts for suspected members of the Lakurawa and Mamudawa groups.

He disclosed that there had reportedly been a disagreement between the two groups following the attacks on worshippers on Friday.

According to him, some members of the groups were said to have opposed the invasion of mosques and abduction of worshippers, leading to clashes between the factions.

He said authorities suspected that the abductors might have targeted youths for recruitment, although it remained unclear whether the attackers were members of Lakurawa or Mamudawa.

In recent months, reports have emerged of suspected Lakurawa fighters operating in parts of Niger State, where they allegedly gathered residents for preaching and warned them against activities they considered contrary to their interpretation of Islamic teachings.

The group has reportedly preached against stealing, alcohol consumption and adultery, while calling on residents to observe Sharia principles.

Despite assurances by security agencies that efforts are ongoing to combat armed groups in Niger State, the latest attacks have further underscored the security challenges confronting communities in the state.

Last week, more than 20 people were reportedly killed in parts of Borgu Local Government Area.

Borgu was also the scene of a major abduction in November 2025, when gunmen reportedly abducted more than 200 pupils in Papiri. The children were later released after spending about a month in captivity.

World.title: Kidnappers flee as police rescue 75 victims in Birnin Gwari
World.content:
Police

By Ibrahim Hassan-Wuyo

KADUNA — The Kaduna State Police Command has rescued 75 kidnapped victims, including men, women and children, abducted by armed men in Folwaya Village, near Birnin Gwari.

The victims, identified as Fulani travellers, were reportedly abducted while travelling in commercial buses on Wednesday.

The Police Public Relations Officer, DSP Mansir Hassan, disclosed this in a statement, saying the incident occurred at about 5:30 p.m. on August 19, 2026, following information received from the Birnin Gwari branch of the National Union of Road Transport Workers (NURTW).

According to him, the victims were abducted by unknown gunmen armed with AK-47 rifles and other sophisticated weapons and taken into a forest.

He said the abductors later concealed the victims in a cave within a mountainous area.

Hassan said that upon receiving the information, a tactical team from the Birnin Gwari Area Command was immediately deployed to the location.

He added that the arrival of the operatives forced the kidnappers to flee, abandoning the victims, who were rescued unharmed.

The Commissioner of Police, Kaduna State Command, CP Rabiu Muhammad, commended the NURTW, Birnin Gwari branch, for providing timely and vital information that facilitated the rescue operation.

He also praised the Area Commander, Birnin Gwari, and his operatives for their swift and professional response.

The CP urged residents to remain vigilant and promptly report suspicious movements and activities to the police.

He, however, cautioned members of the public against taking the law into their own hands, warning that such actions could lead to the loss of innocent lives.

World.title: Liverpool, Man City face questions in new era without Salah, Guardiola
World.content:
Mohamed Salah and Pep Guardiola are two of the most iconic figures in Premier League history — how Liverpool and Manchester City cope without them will define their seasons.

For the first time since 2016, Liverpool kick off a campaign without Egypt forward Salah as their talisman, while City can no longer rely on Guardiola’s managerial genius to inspire them after a glorious decade.

Salah joined Turkish club Trabzonspor earlier in August, ending the Anfield career of one of the greatest players in Liverpool’s illustrious history.

Guardiola resigned at the conclusion of last season, bringing the curtain down on the most successful period in City’s history.

Now Liverpool and City launch new eras without them as the Premier League season gets underway.

City host Bournemouth on Sunday in Enzo Maresca’s first league game as Guardiola’s successor.

Just a few hours later, Liverpool’s new manager Andoni Iraola will pick a team shorn of Salah when the Reds travel to Newcastle.

The uncertainty over the prospects of both City and Liverpool this season is a reflection not only on the loss of Guardiola and Salah, but also the turbulence that preceded their emotional farewells in May.

Guardiola won six Premier League titles and the club’s first Champions League crown among a remarkable 20 trophies after taking charge in 2016.

The 55-year-old lifted the FA Cup and League Cup in his last season, but he exited with City removed from their perch as England’s pre-eminent force after failing to win the title in his final two years.

Guardiola admitted he struggled to generate the energy required to lead City’s fight against Arsenal last term, with the Gunners eventually finishing seven points clear as they clinched the title.

The departure of his trusted director of football Txiki Begiristain in 2025 left Guardiola lamenting “a part of me is leaving”.

With City also fighting against Football Association charges relating to alleged financial breaches — a protracted saga that still doesn’t have a resolution — Guardiola felt he must remain loyal to the club.

But he looked increasingly fatigued by the strain of rebuilding a squad in need of new blood after the departures of several stalwarts including Kevin De Bruyne, Ederson, Kyle Walker and Riyad Mahrez in recent years.

‘Generational talent’

City’s expensively assembled rebuild has been only a partial success, leaving former Chelsea boss Maresca with a daunting task to follow in Guardiola’s footsteps.

The Italian knows City well after working as Guardiola’s assistant in their treble-winning 2022-23 season.

But Maresca has only limited managerial experience after less than two seasons at Chelsea, a year in the second tier with Leicester and a brief stint at Parma.

The 46-year-old’s sparse CV is a far cry from Guardiola’s trophy-filled time at Barcelona and Bayern Munich before his move to Manchester.

Just 35 miles down the East Lancashire Road, Liverpool are also taking tentative steps into season one of their post-Salah story.

When Salah joined Liverpool from Roma for £36 million in 2017, few would have predicted the success that followed.

Salah had flopped during a spell at Chelsea, but he was an immediate hit on Merseyside.

The 34-year-old amassed 257 goals for Liverpool in 442 appearances in all competitions, making him the third top goalscorer in the club’s history.

He produced countless magical moments while winning two Premier League titles, a Champions League and the FA Cup and League Cup.

But the denouement to Salah’s Liverpool career was ugly.

He was dropped several times by Arne Slot last season and accused the club of throwing him “under the bus”.

Salah’s rift with Slot was never fully healed and he scored just seven league goals as Liverpool finished fifth prior to the Dutch coach’s sacking.

Replacing a generational talent of Salah’s status will take more than one player.

Iraola will hope Sweden striker Alexander Isak is much improved after an injury-plagued first season at Anfield, while new signing Victor Munoz and teenager Rio Ngumoha have great expectations.

But no matter how hard they try, neither Liverpool or City will ever be quite the same without their era-defining icons.

World.title: US, Canada fail to reach trade pact to avert Trump tariffs
World.content:
Hefty US tariffs on some Canadian products took effect on Saturday after days of negotiations that went down to the wire failed to produce an agreement.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney vowed that his country will match the US tariffs “dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” as officials said late Friday that Washington and Ottawa had not managed to strike a deal.

The lack of a final agreement means that new 50-percent duties impacting some $20 billion worth of goods, or 5.5 percent of Canadian exports to the United States, came into force.

Impacted products range from hockey sticks to cement.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said Friday that “tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week.”

That came despite Washington’s offers for tariff reductions in sectors like steel and aluminum, he added in a statement.

A senior US official said there are no further scheduled meetings for now.

The surprise announcement came after Trump said that the United States “should be able to have a deal with Canada,” citing his “good relationship” with Carney.

After hours of trade talks on Friday, however, Canada’s top negotiator Dominic LeBlanc told reporters that officials still “have more work to do.”

LeBlanc and Greer also met for around three hours on Thursday.

Greer said that the Trump administration put on the table “significant tariff reductions on steel, aluminum, autos and lumber” in exchange for concessions from Canada.

He said that Canada was also maintaining its “prolonged retaliation” against the United States, including prohibitions on certain American goods and services.

Canada’s regional leaders said previously that the United States was particularly irritated by one retaliatory measure: the removal of US alcohol and wine from liquor stores.

But Carney added in a separate statement that “last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”

While Washington and Ottawa made “important progress” in recent weeks, Carney said, this “has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians.”

The senior US official, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said Canada had sought additional concessions that the United States was unable to provide.

But they added that talks were candid and not acrimonious.

‘Significant pressure’

Ryan Majerus, a former US commerce official, told AFP that “if Canada has agreed to also impose retaliatory tariffs, that will make deescalating this a lot harder.”

“But I think both sides will face significant pressure in the coming days to find an off-ramp,” added Majerus, a trade lawyer with King & Spalding.

Christopher Padilla, another former US official who is now with Brunswick Group, told AFP there has been “a lot of hope among businesses on both sides” for a deal to “turn the page on what has been a very difficult eighteen months in the US-Canada relationship.”

The White House had alleged “discriminatory treatment” by Canada against US alcohol, automobile and dairy products in introducing the duties.

They were originally set to take effect on Wednesday, before Trump issued a last-minute delay of three days, citing major progress in talks.

Canadian negotiators had been camped out in Washington this week to firm up a deal that aimed to address various flash points.

Canada has been seeking relief from Trump’s tariffs on autos, steel and aluminum, which have battered the country’s economy, forced job losses and strained what was once an iron-clad trade relationship.

Carney has repeatedly told Canadians that relations with the United States have been forever changed, regardless of what happens with an individual trade deal.

He says the country must diversify and reduce its reliance on the United States, which currently accounts for roughly 70 percent of Canadian exports.

Beyond the latest tariffs, the United States and Canada still have to agree on revisions to the North American free trade agreement, USMCA, which Trump declined to renew in its current form.

World.title: 100-Day Captives: FG, Borno intensify efforts to rescue 44 pupils
World.content:
Governor of Borno State, Babagana Zulum

The Federal Government and Borno Government have intensified efforts to secure the safe release of 44 schoolchildren abducted from Mussa community in Askira/Uba Local Government Area.

Read Also: 100 days in captivity: Borno families demand rescue of abducted children

Gov. Babagana Zulum disclosed this on Friday when he met with parents of the abducted pupils in Maiduguri.

The meeting followed a request by the parents, who appealed for urgent government intervention to secure the children’s safe release.

Zulum expressed sympathy to the affected families and assured them of President Bola Tinubu’s commitment to rescuing the abducted pupils.

He said Tinubu had directed security agencies to intensify efforts toward ensuring the children’s safe return to their families.

According to him, the Nigerian Armed Forces and Borno Government were working together to achieve the objective.

“On behalf of the government and people of Borno, I once again extend my sympathies over what happened at Mussa Central Primary School,” Zulum said.

He said the incident occurred on May 15, resulting in the abduction of about 44 primary school pupils.

The governor assured the parents that the government would continue doing everything possible to secure the children’s safe return.

The meeting was attended by Sen. Ali Ndume, representing Southern Borno Senatorial District, and other senior government officials.

Those present included commissioners responsible for education and inter-governmental affairs, among other government officials.
