World.title: Missed the deadline? Here’s how to get your cell phone service back
World.content:
The first enforced deadline for compliance with mandatory cell phone registration came and went on Aug. 15 and approximately 2.6 million phone lines were suspended, prompting chaos and confusion for users whose now-unregistered phone numbers end in “0.”

Mexico’s Telecommunications Regulatory Commission (CRT) announced on Thursday that nearly 9.7 million users whose number ends in “0” successfully registered their cell phones before the deadline.

The CRT also said that just over 2.3 million users whose lines had been suspended managed to reactivate their phone service by Aug. 19. Another 2.6 million mobile phones are expected to be reactivated in the coming days, while the CRT expects 2.5 million “unused” lines to be decommissioned.

Those who failed to register before the deadline faced plenty of online misinformation, but those whose service was suspended can still recover their service because their phone number was not canceled.

To reactivate the service, users must complete the registration process via their phone company. Prepaid lines must also be registered to remain active.

You can register through the phone company’s registration portal and by verifying your identity. Links to all providers’ platforms can be found on the CRT website here.

You can also complete the process in person at one of your company’s customer service centers, where staff is on hand to assist with the registration.

Mexican mobile phone owners must provide a CURP (Unique Population Registry Code) and a valid official ID, such as the INE-issued voter ID.

Foreigners must also register their phone lines (if it is a Mexican provider) by using the corresponding identity or immigration document, such as a resident visa or a passport.

Procedures vary slightly depending on the phone company, but the process is free.

It is important to note that suspended lines can still make calls to emergency numbers, citizen services and their phone company. They will also continue to receive earthquake alerts and they can be used to complete the registration process.

The government mandated cell phone registration procedures in an effort to eliminate anonymous mobile lines, stop criminal extortion and curb the use of untraceable “burner” prepaid SIM cards.

The CRT had originally established a June 30 deadline for all cell phones to be registered, but when it became apparent that a significant number of users would see their lines suspended, the deadline was extended.

The official schedule to register cell phones now depends on the final digit of your phone number. If your phone number ends in “1,” you must register by Aug. 31. If it ends in “2,” your deadline is Sept. 15, and so on through the end of the year as shown in the graphic above.

In its Aug. 20 report, the CRT said a total of 73.2 million lines — or 60.5% of the total lines expected to be connected in the country — were registered. By the end of the registration process, it expects a purge of around 25 million lines.

With reports from El Universal, Wired and LatinUS

World.title: Mexico’s urban sprawl is steadily reshaping life in its biggest cities
World.content:
A new study has found that 69 Mexican metropolitan areas nearly doubled their urban populations from 1990 to 2020, but much of that growth occurred farther from the heart of downtown, leaving their central areas with 2.5 million fewer residents.

The study, published July 25 by researchers at Tecnológico de Monterrey’s Center for the Future of Cities (CFC) and the Complexity Science Hub in Vienna, Austria, examined census data from 1990, 2000, 2010 and 2020.

It found that population distribution shifted steadily toward intermediate, distant and peripheral areas.

More than 40% of residents in the metro areas studied lived in central areas in 1990. By 2020, that share had fallen to 22%, according to the research.

Researchers said limited affordable housing in established urban areas — where land and construction costs are higher — helped push growth outward. Cheaper peripheral land and housing policies that favored development outside consolidated areas also contributed to the shift.

Researchers also cited rising car ownership and transportation planning that lagged behind new development as factors that reinforced the pattern.

As a result, a larger share of residents lived farther from jobs, schools, health care and other services — with increased travel times and distances needed to get to those locations from their homes.

In Mexico City, the population of areas nearest the historic center fell by about 166,000 residents during the period, even as the broader metropolitan area grew.

Monterrey’s population within 5 kilometers of its center fell from about 485,000 in 1990 to 377,000 in 2020, while Guadalajara lost more than 200,000 residents in the same radius.

Researchers estimated that the average distance between where residents lived and their city’s center increased 28% as populations moved outward.

The study does not establish whether outward moves were voluntary or involuntary, nor does it identify the income or job location of individual households that moved. It also does not establish gentrification, rent increases or replacement by wealthier residents as a factor in the departures.

Its authors instead focused on documenting the shift.

Alberto Meouchi, head of the Mexico City office of Tec de Monterrey’s CFC, told Wired en Español that a return of all residents to traditional city centers was unrealistic.

He said cities could instead develop multiple centers that bring housing, jobs, services and transportation closer together.

With reports from TecScience, Animal Político, La Silla Rota and Wired

World.title: What I learned from a summer in San Miguel de Allende: 10 reflections from an MND intern
World.content:
Nine weeks ago, I set foot on Mexican soil for the first time in my life. I spent the next two months discovering a small part of the country by traveling, exploring San Miguel, and trying to understand daily life and culture here.

Now it’s time for me to head back to the United States and embark on my senior year of college. I’ll go back feeling like the same person, but with a fresh perspective on life in another country.

Here are my 10 reflections as I end my summer internship with Mexico News Daily.

1. From what I saw, Mexico is nothing like how it is often portrayed in the United States. The only people I saw holding guns were police. I never felt unsafe or witnessed any drug use. What I found instead was gorgeous cities, incredible nature and a warm, friendly populace. I was here in the summer, and it was not even that hot! Mexico gets a bad rap and some of it is justified, but like any large place, the reality is more complicated than any single narrative. Mexico has some of the best destinations in the Western Hemisphere that get overlooked because of its perception in American media.

2. Mexico did not change me, per se. I’m going back to the United States next week feeling like I’m still the same person I was when I left. Would six months in Mexico instead of two have changed that? I don’t know. I could have gone out and interacted with people more. I could have drank more margaritas or gone out of my comfort zone, but I chose to be myself. I still had amazing experiences, travelled around the country and ate some amazing food, but I could have done more to give myself a truly transformative experience.

3. Nothing demonstrated the immaculate vibes of Mexico quite like El Tri’s loss to England in the round of 16. Given soccer’s culture of hooliganism and frequent riots after big game losses in North American sports, I expected a similar reaction from Mexico’s famously passionate fans. But after the final whistle grew, music started blasting out of speakers and people began dancing. I was shocked. This was a monumental opportunity for Mexico soccer and they lost. Most fans would be crushed and would let it ruin their week. But the Mexican fans danced and sang.

4. Mexico has lots of scary bugs. I hate bugs. On the couple of excursions I made to San Miguel de Allende’s botanical gardens, I witnessed some of the creepiest looking beetles I’ve ever seen in my life — never mind the giant hornets, massive red ants, or constant threat of scorpions (which I’m thankful I never saw.) Coming face to face with freaky bugs may have been my least favorite part of my Mexico experience.

5. Catholicism is visible everywhere in Mexico, but it does not create a society as conservative as one might think. While in San Miguel, I attended the local pride parade and in Mexico City I saw pride flags everywhere. Many people take their religious beliefs seriously, but Mexicans are generally understanding and welcoming.

6. The lack of polarization was a breath of fresh air. While riding on a long bus to Mexico City, I was getting to know my coworker and travelling companion, María. We disagreed on a lot of political issues and even on ideologies, but it never had any effect on our relationship. I can be “woke” while she is not. With the extremism ever-present in the U.S., this might be a dealbreaker. But in Mexico, it’s just differences I have with a friend.

7. This one may be obvious, but the food lives up to the hype.

8. Mexico is generally more laid back than their northern neighbors. As a night owl and a late riser, I tended to like that. But when I had to wait a long time for food at restaurants and there is less urgency in customer service, I sometimes found myself missing American customer service. Even the local McDonalds felt like it took forever.

9. As a massive introvert, I really enjoyed living by myself away from almost everyone I knew, but it had its drawbacks. I was too shy to go to bars most of the time, even though the bar scene in San Miguel is active late into the night. Most nights I did not have many regrets, but by the end, part of me wished I had made more friends.

10. Mexico may not have changed who I am, but it has had a major impact on my life. Living in a different country taught me new ways to communicate and new ways to think. I got a front-row seat to the lives completely different from my own, which was equal parts fascinating and harrowing. I’ll never forget Hierve el Agua or Monte Albán in Oaxaca, or witnessing Mexico beat Ecuador with hundreds of thousands of people in the Zócalo in Mexico City. I’m going back the same person, but these nine weeks will have a lasting impact on me.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Despite surging peso, further interest rate cuts remain unlikely for the foreseeable future
World.content:
The Bank of Mexico adopted a guarded approach in its Aug. 6-7 monetary policy meeting, indicating it is likely to keep its benchmark interest unchanged, even as inflation is easing.

In minutes from the meeting released on Thursday, the central bank cited an uncertain global backdrop and lingering inflation risks in its decision to maintain a 6.5% interest rate, deeming it “adequate to face the current economic risks.”

It further justified maintaining the rate by assessing “the observed levels of the [peso-dollar] exchange rate, the absence of demand pressures in the economy and the degree of monetary restriction implemented.”

The board said it believed the monetary policy stance “is adequate to meet the challenges of the macroeconomic environment, including those arising from the international context.”

Still, four of the five members of Banxico’s Governing Board said the persistence of inflation in services remains a concern, prompting the cautious stance. A balance of risks skewed to the upside and the continued weakness of the Mexican economy also impacted the decision.

Policymakers view inflation in services (i.e., restaurants, hotels and air travel) as a key concern as it has remained above 4% since late 2021. It is viewed as one of the primary obstacles to bringing overall inflation back to the bank’s 3% target.

Board members attributed lingering price pressures in the service sector to businesses adjusting prices slowly while facing elevated costs for labor and living expenses

Headline inflation slowed to 3.12% in July, down from 3.37% in June, marking its lowest level since May 2020. However, core inflation — which excludes some volatile food and energy prices — registered at 3.95%, down slightly from 4.03% in June.

Banxico, as the Banco de México is also known, now says it doesn’t expect headline inflation to converge to its 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027, requiring sustained monetary discipline. In the short term, analysts surveyed by Banxico expect year-end headline inflation of 4.00%.

A strong peso has helped curb inflation. The currency — hovering at and below 17 to the U.S. dollar since last week — has strengthened nearly 6% in 2026, helped considerably by a weaker dollar, though ⁠Mexico’s solid macroeconomic fundamentals are a factor as well.

The minutes noted that the economy expanded in the second quarter (+1.5%) after contracting in the first, but some members warned that weakness persists in various components of demand.

Regarding the international environment, the board highlighted tensions in the Middle East that continue to pose upside risks to inflation, cautioning that the prolonged conflict has tested the buffers that “have mitigated the rise in oil prices.”

With reports from Reuters, El Economista, Forbes México and Mexico Business News

World.title: El Jalapeño: Mexico City officials petition Nobel Peace Prize committee on behalf of conchas
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

MEXICO CITY — Fresh off securing local Intangible Cultural Heritage status for pan dulce, municipal authorities confirmed Tuesday they have submitted a preliminary diplomatic petition urging the Norwegian Nobel Committee to create a new Peace Prize category explicitly reserved for baked goods.

The initiative, spearheaded jointly by city cultural representatives and baking industry executives, argues that the diplomatic potential of a warm concha served alongside a cup of café de olla remains criminally underutilized in global conflict resolution. Officials cited preliminary municipal data suggesting that 94% of domestic arguments end immediately upon the introduction of a fresh besito or oreja.

“We respect the committee’s historical focus on multilateral treaties and international disarmament,” said lead policy strategist Mateo Morales during a press briefing at a historic downtown bakery. “However, bilateral negotiations routinely stall because delegates are hungry and irritable. A structured, mandatory coffee break featuring artisanal sweet bread provides a proven framework for immediate de-escalation.”

Under the proposed guidelines submitted to Oslo, negotiators facing high-stakes diplomatic deadlocks would be legally required to pause proceedings, dip a traditional concha into warm milk, and reassess their geopolitical demands before resuming talks. Municipal analysts calculated that this protocol alone could reduce global diplomatic friction by up to 40%.

Industry representatives supported the initiative, noting that while standard diplomatic accords require months of complex drafting, a well-timed tray of marranitos achieves consensus in under three minutes. They added that the initiative would include comprehensive technical support for foreign embassies seeking to implement proper dunking methodologies.

City officials acknowledged that expanding the Nobel criteria to include pastries faces procedural hurdles in Stockholm and Oslo, but noted they remain prepared to send a diplomatic delegation equipped with fresh trays of pan de muerto to expedite the review process.

World.title: Extradited Navy offficer, accused of fuel-trafficking, arrives from Argentina to Mexico’s top security prison
World.content:
Alleged fuel smuggler Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna arrived from Argentina on Friday and is now incarcerated at the Altiplano maximum security prison in México state.

Farías — accused of leading a network that siphoned off millions in profits from state oil company Pemex — will face an initial arraignment hearing ahead of what promises to be explosive judicial proceedings.

Fernando “N”, posiblemente relacionado con una compleja red criminal dedicada al contrabando, dispersión y distribución de combustible, es trasladado a México. pic.twitter.com/A96Bh8ToZt — FGR México (@FGRMexico) August 20, 2026

After months on the run, Farías was arrested in Buenos Aires in April for entering Argentina with a fake passport. Two petitions for asylum were rejected and his challenges against extradition were turned aside. His departure has been categorized as an administrative expulsion.

His brother Manuel Roberto Farías Laguna, a former vice admiral, has been in prison since September 2025. The sibling high-ranking Navy officers allegedly ran a corruption network across several customs posts.

The network was finally exposed in March 2025 and federal authorities swept up 14 suspects — including Manuel Roberto — six months later.

Further heightening the intrigue, the Farías Laguna were nephews of Admiral Rafael Ojeda Durán, the Navy minister during the Andrés Manuel López Obrador administration (2018-2024).

A rear admiral who had reported the scheme to Admiral Ojeda in June 2024 was murdered in November of that year under mysterious circumstances.

Then-Attorney General Alejandro Gertz defended Ojeda’s integrity, saying the admiral himself had approached the authorities to request an investigation into some of the naval officers assigned to custom posts, although no evidence of any such investigation was made public.

The Farías Laguna case has dealt a serious blow to the reputation of the Navy, which had long been considered more disciplined and more reliable than the Army, which has dealt with its fair share of corruption scandals and allegations of human‑rights abuses.

The FGR has built its case against the Farías brothers with testimony from a protected witness known as “Santo,” who claims the suspects controlled the appointment of subordinates in customs offices (which are controlled by the Navy) and paid them substantial bribes.

Once the case goes to trial, Fernando Farías’s defense counsel is expected to summon Ojeda and argue that Farías was a subordinate in the corruption network. The defense is likely to add further fuel to the fire by alluding to allegations that Andrés Manuel López Beltrán — the son of the former president — is linked to the smuggling network.

President Claudia Sheinbaum this week rejected the suggestion that López Beltrán was involved in criminal activity.

The defense has also argued that the United States improperly intervened in Farías’s expulsion from Argentina.

With reports from La Jornada, EFE, El País and SDP Noticias

World.title: Mexico rejects US decision to deport Mexicans to Central America: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Today’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🌡️ Sheinbaum sits out press conference: Early on Friday, the president announced she woke up with “very bad flu, cough and fever” and was told by doctors to rest. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez and INAH chief Joel Omar Vázquez led the conference in her place. Sheinbaum said she expected to resume activities the next day.

Early on Friday, the president announced she woke up with “very bad flu, cough and fever” and was told by doctors to rest. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez and INAH chief Joel Omar Vázquez led the conference in her place. Sheinbaum said she expected to resume activities the next day. 🏺 INAH reveals discoveries in Chiapas cave: Vázquez said archaeologists found 13 offerings and 179 pre-Hispanic pieces this year in the Mundo Zoque cave, a Zoque pilgrimage site used to request rain and good harvests. Highlights include ceramics from the late Classic Period (600–900 AD) and an incense burner featuring a quincunx design.

Vázquez said archaeologists found 13 offerings and 179 pre-Hispanic pieces this year in the Mundo Zoque cave, a Zoque pilgrimage site used to request rain and good harvests. Highlights include ceramics from the late Classic Period (600–900 AD) and an incense burner featuring a quincunx design. 🇺🇸 🛬 Mexico objects to deportations to Central America: Rodríguez said she told U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to send some Mexican deportees to Central America rather than Mexico.

Rodríguez said she told U.S. Ambassador Ronald Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to send some Mexican deportees to Central America rather than Mexico. 📈 Rodríguez touts July growth data: The interior minister called INEGI’s preliminary estimate of 2.7% annual GDP growth in July “yet another piece of good news,” following 2.1% growth in Q2.

Why today’s mañanera matters

At 6:01 a.m. Friday, President Claudia Sheinbaum announced on social media that she had woken up with “very bad flu, cough and fever.”

“It’s nothing serious, but doctors have recommended rest, so today’s [press] conference will be organized by Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez Velázquez and the general director of the National Institute of Anthropology and History, Joel Omar Vázquez Herrera,” she wrote.

Les informo que amanecí con gripa muy fuerte, tos y fiebre; no es nada grave, pero los médicos me han recomendado reposo, por lo que la conferencia de hoy estará coordinada por la secretaria de Gobernación, Rosa Icela Rodríguez Velázquez, y el director general del INAH, Joel Omar… — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) August 21, 2026

“Don’t miss it, they will talk about archaeological discoveries. I’m sure that tomorrow I’ll resume my activities. An affectionate hug from afar,” Sheinbaum wrote.

Later on Friday morning, Vázquez spoke about recent discoveries in a subterranean cave in the southern state of Chiapas.

Rodríguez subsequently provided a headline for media outlets by revealing that she had told U.S. Ambassador to Mexico Ronald Johnson that Mexico doesn’t agree with the Trump administration’s decision to send some Mexican deportees to Central America.

Also of note at today’s mañanera was the interior minister’s response to data showing that the Mexican economy performed solidly in July.

Discoveries in the ‘Mundo Zoque’ Cave

Vázquez spoke about discoveries archaeologists have made in the Mundo Zoque (Zoque World) Cave, a cave in the municipality of Cintalapa, Chiapas, that is named after the Indigenous Zoque people.

The cave, Vázquez explained, was a pilgrimage site where Zoque people went to “request rain and good harvests.”

The INAH chief said that in the first half of this year, archaeologists discovered 13 ofrendas (offerings) in the cave along with 179 pre-Hispanic pieces, including ceramic bowls.

Vázquez said that INAH has determined that the ceramic pieces were made in the late Classic Period — i.e. between 600 and 900 B.C. He said that the pieces include images of jaguars, tecolotes (a kind of owl), “human representations and plant motives.”

Vázquez highlighted that one of the pieces found by archaeologists is a sahumador (incense burner) with a 32-centimeter-long handle. The incense burner’s plate features “the image of a quincunx, a figure that alludes to the four directions of the universe,” he said, noting also that the end of the handle is adorned with a snake design.

“It’s a sublime piece, a very beautiful piece that is representative of the Zoque culture,” Vázquez said.

He said that archeologists also found stalactites and stalagmites in the cave that had been “modified to look like human figures or the jaws of the monster of the earth.”

Rodríguez: Mexico doesn’t agree with US decision to send Mexican deportees to Central America

Rodríguez told reporters that her meeting with Ambassador Johnson on Thursday focused on migration.

She said that she and the ambassador spoke about the reduction in “irregular migration” to the United States of both Mexicans and nationals of other countries.

“It has declined 96%,” Rodríguez said, apparently referring to the monthly average of illegal crossings during the Trump administration compared to the monthly average during the Biden administration.

The interior minister subsequently noted that the United States has deported some Mexicans to Central American countries.

The Trump administration has been quietly deporting migrants from Mexico to Honduras and Guatemala, despite the Mexican government’s willingness to accept the return of all its citizens, Homeland Security sources tell CBS News’ @camiloreports. pic.twitter.com/qe84ZJNpxi — CBS News (@CBSNews) August 19, 2026

As a result of “this new U.S. decision,” Mexicans have been sent to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica, Rodríguez said. She said she told Johnson that Mexico respects the migration policy decisions of other countries, “but we don’t agree with our compatriots being sent to a third country.”

“… We spoke about this firmly, respectfully but firmly, in order to say that we don’t agree with this decision,” Rodríguez said.

Rodríguez celebrates solid economic growth in July

A reporter noted that INEGI published preliminary data showing that the Mexican economy grew 2.7% in annual terms in July. The publication of the data on Thursday came three weeks after INEGI reported annual growth of 2.1% in the second quarter of 2026. Annual growth in the first quarter was just 0.4%, and the Mexican economy contracted on a sequential basis in that period.

Rodríguez said that the growth data for July is “yet another piece of good news” for the Mexican economy.

“… It’s a very good indicator,” she said.

“… It’s another good result of the government of President Claudia Sheinbaum, and we’re going to continue on this same path,” Rodríguez said.

World.title: MND Local: New flights, fashion charity and Michin Aquarium in Guadalajara
World.content:
This week in Guadalajara, we look at the four new international routes being added at Miguel Hidalgo International Airport, the charitable activities of BRED and a great opportunity to visit the Michin Aquarium at a reduced cost.

While foreign airlines pull back, Volaris keeps expanding service in Guadalajara

We recently reported on Canadian carrier WestJet’s elimination of the new Guadalajara-Calgary nonstop route for the coming winter. Fortunately for Tapatíos, new routes will be arriving in its place starting in December.

The ultra-low-cost carrier (ULCC in industry jargon) will expand its service at Miguel Hidalgo International Airport this winter to the U.S. East Coast, along with two new international routes in Latin America.

Volaris’ new U.S. nonstop routes are from Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport (ATL) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD). The carrier’s new southbound routes are to José María Córdova International Airport (MDE) in Medellín, Colombia, and La Aurora International Airport (GUA) in Guatemala City.

Three of those four flights are new nonstop routes for Guadalajara, the exception being the Atlanta route, already served by Delta Air Lines. The move cements Guadalajara as a strategic domestic hub for the airline. Volaris now services 60 destinations with more than 110 daily departures from Jalisco’s capital.

A growing network of connections

The new services reflect the Mexican carrier’s broader push to grow its U.S. network and increase its market share. Over the past year, Volaris has increased its U.S. network capacity by 12%, even as the overall market has contracted. From Guadalajara, Volaris offered 17.4% more seats in summer 2026 compared with summer 2025. Its rapid growth over this period drove its share of total capacity at GDL from 53% to nearly 60%.

Volaris’ new routes to Medellín and Guatemala City will provide meaningful improvement for southbound travel from Guadalajara, as the new routes eliminate the obligatory stop in Mexico City and should cut travel time in half. They are a welcome complement to Volaris’ existing nonstop service to Bogotá, Colombia, and San José, Costa Rica, from La Perla Tapatía.

BRED gives new life to the fashion industry’s mounds of unsold clothing

At the recently concluded Intermoda trade show for the fashion industry here in Guadalajara, local businessman Sergio López de la Cerda had more than the latest trends on his mind.

López de la Cerda was intent on making contacts and finding companies with excess goods to donate to the charitable organization he runs, The Clothing and Household Goods Bank of Guadalajara. Better known to locals as simply BRED, the organization’s mission is to distribute apparel, furniture and housewares to economically disadvantaged local families.

“What we are looking for is to link companies that manufacture clothing, that manufacture furniture or the marketers of these products, so that they can donate products to us, and we will take them directly to the families (who need it),” he told El Economista in a recent interview.

Leveraging a network of local textile, clothing, footwear and furniture producers, BRED is helping to reduce product waste while addressing a pressing social need.

Not the latest fashions, but fashions nonetheless

At Intermoda, López de la Cerda pointed out that many of the donated garments have no commercial value but are still perfectly usable. “Companies donate … clothing from a season that has already passed,” he explained.

If not for the involvement of social welfare groups, these unwanted goods would most likely end up in landfills. The silver lining for manufacturers and retailers is an opportunity to burnish their public image while reducing waste in their supply chains.

Clothing and household items collected by BRED are distributed through the logistics network of the Guadalajara Food Bank, which already had the infrastructure in place.

According to López de la Cerda, the organization now provides support to 338 communities in 81 municipalities in Jalisco, with regular donations of food, clothing, footwear, furniture and other basic items. It makes a meaningful contribution to helping improve the daily lives of an estimated 1.2 million Jalisco residents experiencing food insecurity.

BRED donation centers encourage public participation

To complement the goods donated by the business sector, BRED’s leadership seeks to boost citizen participation in its efforts. To this end, it operates more than 25 donation centers across the Guadalajara metropolitan area, where people can drop off clothing in good condition to help local families in need.

“We want families to bring in clothes they no longer use, as long as they are in good condition, so we can process them and send them directly to those who need them most,” López de la Cerda said.

Take the family on an underwater adventure without leaving the city

The Michin Aquarium is offering a deal to wrap up the summer season. From Aug. 14-30, 2026, entrance fees start at just 99 pesos per person, making a sea adventure accessible to those looking for affordable family fun right here in town.

Since 2017, the Michin Aquarium has been operating in Guadalajara’s historic center next to Alcalde Park. It houses approximately 10,000 marine organisms and serves as an important rescue, education and conservation center in western Mexico. The facility drew acclaim from conservationists back in 2018 as the first in Mexico to successfully breed neotropical river otters.

Popular exhibits include a vast oceanarium featuring bull sharks, nurse sharks and stingrays, which visitors experience up close by strolling through a glass tunnel. Additional exhibits showcase the variety of Mexican water habitats that are home to exotic jellyfish, technicolor reef fish, pink flamingos, crocodiles and more.

If that isn’t enough, a recently added petting zoo with capybaras and miniature pigs is sure to please the little ones.

Dates: The summer promotion runs Aug. 14-30, 2026.

Location: Calle Mariano Bárcena 990, Zona Centro, 44260 Guadalajara.

Cost: Tickets are available on the aquarium’s website, starting at 99 pesos.

MND Writer Dawn Stoner is reporting from Guadalajara.

World.title: Pablo Marçal Loses Two More Appeals and Stays Barred to 2032
World.content:
Brazil · ELECTIONS

Key Facts — TRE-SP ruling On 5 August 2026, the São Paulo regional electoral court unanimously rejected Marçal’s clarification appeal, keeping his eight-year ineligibility.

— TSE measures Barred from public campaign funds and from TV and radio slots, pending judgment on his 2026 candidacy

— Clean Record Law The ineligibility stems from improper use of media during the 2024 campaign, under the Lei da Ficha Limpa.

— Timeline The eight-year ban counts from the 2024 elections, making Marçal ineligible until 2032.

— Current status Marçal has filed for president in 2026; his registration appears as awaiting judgment.

The former presidential hopeful remains barred from elected office until 2032, even as his 2026 candidacy awaits judgment at the higher court.

The Superior Electoral Court in Brasília. Its measures on campaign funds run separately from the eight-year ineligibility imposed by the São Paulo court. (Photo: O Tribunal da Democracia, Public domain, Wikimedia Commons.)

Pablo Marçal remains barred from elected office until 2032 after losing two more appeals in August 2026. The São Paulo regional electoral court and its president rejected his requests, keeping the eight-year ineligibility intact.

Two Appeals Rejected

On Wednesday 5 August 2026 the São Paulo regional electoral court rejected a clarification appeal from Pablo Marçal’s defence. The vote was unanimous.

The 7-0 vote kept in place the decision making him ineligible for eight years. Then, on Friday 21 August 2026, the president of the TRE-SP, José Antonio Encinas Manfré, rejected a special appeal by Marçal.

He also refused to admit that appeal to the higher court.

What the Appeals Meant

The clarification appeal, known as embargos de declaração, asks a court to clear up contradictions or omissions in its own ruling. The special appeal, or recurso especial, asks a higher court to review the law applied.

In this case, both were rejected, so the eight-year ineligibility stands. However, coverage of the 5 August ruling said an appeal to the Superior Electoral Court was still possible.

The Basis for Ineligibility

The ineligibility rests on a São Paulo electoral court decision for improper use of the media during the 2024 municipal campaign. This falls under the Clean Record Law, the Lei da Ficha Limpa.

It bars people convicted of certain offences from standing for office for eight years. The eight years count from the 2024 elections, which makes Pablo Marçal ineligible until 2032.

That means he cannot run for any elected position during that period.

Separate Track at the TSE

Meanwhile, a separate track runs at the Superior Electoral Court, the TSE. In mid to late August 2026, the TSE handled his presidential registration and campaign conditions.

The TSE issued precautionary measures barring him from public campaign funds and from television and radio campaign slots and debates. Still, those TSE measures do not change the eight-year ineligibility imposed by the TRE-SP.

Presidential Candidacy Filed

Despite being ineligible until 2032, Pablo Marçal has filed his candidacy for president in 2026. In the official system, it appears as awaiting judgment, while prosecutors and the court decide whether to reject the registration.

So, the TSE has not rejected his candidacy yet. Instead, it is pending a final decision.

Previous Case Overturned

In November 2025 the TRE-SP overturned a first-instance eight-year ineligibility against him on appeal. That was a separate case tied to the 2024 mayoral race.

However, the current ineligibility comes from other electoral court decisions tied to the 2024 elections. Therefore, that overturned case does not affect the current ban.

The current ban remains in force.

What This Means for 2026

For now, Pablo Marçal’s presidential bid is in limbo. Because the TSE has issued precautionary measures, he cannot use public funds or access broadcast slots.

Even so, his name may still appear on ballots if the TSE does not reject his registration. But the eight-year ineligibility from the TRE-SP remains a major hurdle.

Legal Path Ahead

Although the TRE-SP president declined to send the special appeal up, other legal avenues might exist. For example, Marçal could potentially file new appeals or seek other remedies.

Nevertheless, the current decisions keep him barred until 2032. As a result, his political future remains uncertain.

Pablo Marçal’s Status

In short, Pablo Marçal is barred from elected office until 2032, despite his 2026 presidential filing. The TSE’s precautionary measures add further restrictions, but they do not lift the ban.

Overall, the legal situation is complex, with multiple courts involved. Still, the core fact is that his ineligibility stands.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why is Pablo Marçal ineligible until 2032?

He was found guilty of improper use of the media during the 2024 municipal campaign, under the Clean Record Law. The eight-year ban counts from the 2024 elections, so it lasts until 2032.

Did the TSE reject his presidential candidacy?

No, the TSE has not rejected his candidacy. It is awaiting judgment, and the TSE has issued precautionary measures, such as barring him from public campaign funds and TV/radio slots.

What is the difference between the TRE-SP and the TSE?

The TRE-SP is the São Paulo regional electoral court, which imposed the eight-year ineligibility. The TSE is the Superior Electoral Court, which handles his presidential registration and has issued separate precautionary measures.

Can Pablo Marçal still run for president in 2026?

He has filed his candidacy, but it is pending judgment. The eight-year ineligibility from the TRE-SP remains a major obstacle, and the TSE has not yet made a final decision.

Sources: TRE-SP; TSE; Brazilian legal and political press.

World.title: Datafolha State Polls: Big Leads in São Paulo, Rio and Minas
World.content:
Brazil · ELECTIONS

Key Facts — São Paulo Tarcísio de Freitas leads with 45% against Fernando Haddad’s 27%

— Rio de Janeiro Eduardo Paes has 41%, Douglas Ruas 19%, Anthony Garotinho 9%

— Minas Gerais Cleitinho Azevedo leads with 32% in the first round

— Polling dates Fieldwork for all three ran between 18 and 21 August 2026

— Registration Each poll is registered with the electoral court, as required by Brazilian law

With the October vote approaching, the latest surveys show clear front-runners in three of Brazil’s most populous states.

The Palácio dos Bandeirantes, seat of the São Paulo state government. Datafolha puts Tarcísio de Freitas on 45% and Fernando Haddad on 27%. (Photo: Secretaria de Agricultura e Abastecimento, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Datafolha state polls show big leads in São Paulo, Rio and Minas Gerais ahead of the October elections. The surveys, published on Friday 21 August 2026, were conducted for Folha and TV Globo.

São Paulo Governor Race

In São Paulo, incumbent governor Tarcísio de Freitas has 45% support, while Fernando Haddad trails with 27%. If the race goes to a runoff, Tarcísio leads 54% to 35%.

The fieldwork for this poll took place on 18 and 19 August 2026, with a sample of 1,610 people. The margin of error is 2 percentage points, and the poll is registered as SP-01806/2026 and BR-07185/2026.

Rio de Janeiro Governor Race

In Rio de Janeiro, mayor Eduardo Paes leads with 41% of the vote. Douglas Ruas follows with 19%, and Anthony Garotinho has 9%.

The poll was conducted between 18 and 21 August 2026, with a sample of 1,204 people. Its margin of error is 3 percentage points, and it is registered as RJ-02945/2026.

Minas Gerais Governor Race

In Minas Gerais, Cleitinho Azevedo leads the first round with 32% support. The poll ran from 18 to 20 August 2026, with a sample of 1,204 people.

The margin of error here is also 3 percentage points, and the poll is registered as MG-00446/2026. No runoff figures were released for this state.

What the Numbers Mean

A margin of error of 3 points means the true figure is likely within 3 points either side of the reported number. Therefore, the leads in Rio and Minas are significant but not insurmountable.

In São Paulo, however, Tarcísio’s 18-point lead in the first round is well outside the 2-point margin of error. As a result, his advantage looks solid.

The Candidates

Tarcísio de Freitas is the sitting governor of São Paulo. Fernando Haddad is a former mayor of the city and served as finance minister.

Eduardo Paes is the mayor of Rio de Janeiro. Cleitinho Azevedo’s background was not detailed in the poll release.

Still, his lead in Minas Gerais puts him in a strong position.

How the Elections Work

Brazil holds state and federal elections in October 2026. Governors are elected in a first round, with a runoff between the top two if nobody passes 50%.

Because none of the leaders in these polls exceed 50%, runoffs are likely in all three states. In São Paulo, the runoff would be between Tarcísio and Haddad.

Poll Registration

Every published poll in Brazil must be registered with the electoral court, which is why each carries a registration number. This requirement ensures transparency and accountability.

For example, the São Paulo poll has two registration numbers, while Rio and Minas each have one. These numbers allow the public to verify the poll’s details.

Datafolha State Polls Context

The Datafolha state polls come just over a month before the October elections. They provide a snapshot of voter intentions in three key states.

In addition, these polls were conducted for Folha and TV Globo, two major Brazilian media outlets. Their results are widely reported and discussed.

What Happens Next

World.title: Silvinei Vasques Loses His Pension After Coup Conviction

— Judge Justice Alexandre de Moraes

— Conviction date December 2025

— Total sentence 24 years and six months in prison plus 120 day-fines

— Crimes coup d’état, abolition of the democratic rule of law, aggravated damage, deterioration of listed heritage, criminal organisation

The ruling strips the former PRF chief of his retirement income, adding a financial penalty to his 24-year prison sentence.

The Supreme Federal Court in Brasília. Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered the cancellation of the pension on 21 August 2026. (Photo: Joehawkins, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

Silvinei Vasques, the former director-general of Brazil’s Federal Highway Police, has lost his police pension after a coup conviction. On 21 August 2026, Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered the cancellation of Silvinei Vasques’s pension, according to the Supreme Federal Court.

The Pension Cancellation Order

Justice Alexandre de Moraes, who oversees the coup cases at the Supreme Federal Court, issued the order. The decision holds that the penalty of loss of public office reaches his status as a retired officer.

That penalty was already imposed in his criminal case. Therefore, the pension is cancelled as part of that penalty.

No pension amount was stated in the reporting.

Legal Basis for the Decision

The legal basis is the loss of public office penalty. The First Panel of the Supreme Federal Court fixed it in his conviction.

In addition, the decision clarifies that this penalty applies even after retirement. As a result, the cancellation of the pension is the way to carry out that penalty.

This is a straightforward application of the court’s earlier ruling.

Conviction for Coup Attempt

The Supreme Federal Court convicted Silvinei Vasques in December 2025. He was found guilty of taking part in the attempted coup after the 2022 elections.

His total sentence is 24 years and six months in prison, in the closed regime, plus 120 day-fines. The crimes listed include coup d’état, abolition of the democratic rule of law, aggravated damage, deterioration of listed heritage, and criminal organisation.

These are serious charges that reflect the gravity of the case.

Role as PRF Director-General

Silvinei Vasques was the director-general of the Federal Highway Police, known as the PRF. The Federal Highway Police patrol Brazil’s federal roads.

Meanwhile, his position gave him significant authority over federal road operations. However, that authority is now gone, along with his pension.

Understanding Day-Fines

A day-fine is a penalty calculated as a number of days multiplied by a daily rate tied to the convicted person’s income. In this case, the court imposed 120 day-fines.

For example, the exact amount depends on the daily rate set by the court. Still, the day-fine system aims to make the penalty proportional to the offender’s financial situation.

Role of the Supreme Federal Court

The Supreme Federal Court, the STF, is Brazil’s highest court. Alexandre de Moraes is the justice overseeing the coup cases.

In fact, the First Panel of the STF handled the conviction. Consequently, the pension cancellation follows directly from that panel’s decision.

Impact on Retirement Status

The decision explicitly extends the loss of public office to his retired status. Even so, the pension is cancelled because the penalty applies to the office itself.

Once the office is lost, the retirement benefits tied to that office are also lost. This is a key point of the ruling.

Broader Implications for Coup Cases

This ruling sets a precedent for how the STF handles pensions of convicted officials. Although this case involves one individual, the principle could apply to others.

However, the decision is specific to Silvinei Vasques and his circumstances. Still, it shows that the court is willing to enforce financial consequences beyond prison time.

Next Steps for Silvinei Vasques

Silvinei Vasques now faces the loss of his pension on top of his prison sentence. The court’s order is clear and immediate.

In short, the former police chief must deal with the financial impact of his conviction. The decision is part of the ongoing legal aftermath of the coup attempt.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Silvinei Vasques do?

Silvinei Vasques was convicted for taking part in the attempted coup after the 2022 elections. His crimes include coup d’état, abolition of the democratic rule of law, aggravated damage, deterioration of listed heritage, and criminal organisation.

Why was his pension cancelled?

The pension was cancelled because the penalty of loss of public office applies to his retired status. Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered the cancellation on 21 August 2026.

How long is Silvinei Vasques’s prison sentence?

He received a total sentence of 24 years and six months in prison, in the closed regime, plus 120 day-fines. The sentence was handed down by the Supreme Federal Court in December 2025.

What is a day-fine?

A day-fine is a penalty calculated as a number of days multiplied by a daily rate tied to the convicted person’s income. In this case, the court imposed 120 day-fines.

Sources: Supreme Federal Court filings; Brazilian legal press.

World.title: The 6×1 Work Schedule Moves a Step Closer to Ending in Brazil
World.content:
Brazil · WORK

Key Facts — Proposal PEC 221/2019

— Senate step Sent to CCJ committee in mid-August 2026

— Rapporteur Senator Omar Aziz (PSD-AM)

— Chamber approval Passed in May 2026

— Transition period 60 days under Senate discussion

Six days on, one day off, could give way to a 40-hour week and two days of rest.

Inside the Federal Senate in Brasília. PEC 221/2019 is now with the constitution and justice committee, with Omar Aziz as rapporteur. (Photo: Agência Senado, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The 6×1 work schedule moves a step closer to ending in Brazil as the Senate begins formal review of a constitutional amendment. Senator Davi Alcolumbre, president of the Senate, sent the proposal to the constitution and justice committee (CCJ) in mid-August 2026.

What Is the 6×1 Work Schedule?

The 6×1 work schedule means six consecutive days of work and only one day of rest each week. This arrangement is common in many sectors across Brazil, often affecting retail and service workers.

The proposed amendment, known as PEC 221/2019, would end this pattern. It would cut the maximum working week from 44 hours to 40 hours, with no reduction in pay.

Senate Committee Takes Up the Proposal

Senate President Davi Alcolumbre sent PEC 221/2019 to the constitution and justice committee, the CCJ. That happened around 14 to 15 August 2026.

This step came after the Chamber of Deputies had already approved the text. A week later, on Friday 21 August 2026, the committee got its rapporteur.

He is Senator Omar Aziz, of the PSD in Amazonas. The rapporteur writes the committee’s opinion, which shapes what colleagues vote on.

Key Changes Proposed by the Amendment

PEC 221/2019 would abolish the 6×1 schedule. It sets 5×2 as the national reference, meaning five days of work and two of rest.

It guarantees at least two paid rest days a week, with one preferably on Sunday. In addition, the amendment sets a floor of 40 hours per week.

It does not abolish collective bargaining on specific rosters. Special schedules stay possible, as long as the average of two paid rest days holds within the same month.

Chamber of Deputies Approval

The Chamber of Deputies approved PEC 221/19 in first and second rounds on Wednesday 27 May 2026. This approval included a 60-day transition period after promulgation.

However, the Senate is now discussing whether to remove that transition period. On 1 July 2026, G1 reported that Alcolumbre argued for immediate effect, but this is not yet a confirmed change.

Senate President’s Priorities

Alcolumbre has listed the amendment among his priority items. He said on 12 August 2026 that he would talk to senators about moving it forward.

Therefore, the dispatch to the CCJ and the naming of a rapporteur are concrete steps. Still, no voting date has been set, and the timeline remains open.

Understanding the Legislative Process

A PEC, or proposta de emenda à Constituição, is a proposed constitutional amendment. In Brazil, it needs approval in two rounds in both chambers of Congress.

The CCJ is the first stop in the Senate. The rapporteur’s opinion will guide the committee’s decision, which then goes to the full Senate floor.

What Happens Next?

The CCJ will now review the amendment, with Senator Omar Aziz as rapporteur. His opinion will be crucial, as it shapes the text that senators vote on.

Meanwhile, the discussion over the transition period continues. If the Senate removes the 60-day transition, the changes would take effect immediately on promulgation.

That is still under debate.

Potential Impact on Workers

The end of the 6×1 work schedule would give workers more rest days. It would also reduce the maximum working hours without cutting pay, a significant change for many.

For example, workers in sectors with special schedules could still have Sundays or Saturdays worked, but they would need to be compensated. The average of two paid rest days per week must be maintained within the same month.

Final Thoughts on the 6×1 Work Schedule

The 6×1 work schedule is a step closer to ending, but the process is not complete. The Senate’s review will determine the final shape of the amendment.

In short, the proposal has cleared the Chamber and is now in the Senate’s hands. The coming weeks will show how senators handle this significant change to Brazil’s labor rules.

Frequently Asked Questions

What does the 6×1 work schedule mean?

The 6×1 work schedule means six consecutive days of work and only one day of rest each week. This is a common pattern in many jobs in Brazil.

What is PEC 221/2019?

PEC 221/2019 is a proposed constitutional amendment that would abolish the 6×1 schedule. It would reduce the maximum working week from 44 hours to 40 hours without cutting pay.

Who is the rapporteur for the amendment in the Senate?

Senator Omar Aziz of the PSD party in Amazonas was named rapporteur on 21 August 2026. He will write the committee’s opinion on the amendment.

Has the transition period been removed?

No, the transition period is still under discussion. The Chamber’s version includes a 60-day transition, but the Senate is considering removing it.

Sources: Brazilian Senate; G1; Agência Senado; Diap.

Datafolha, the polling institute of the newspaper Folha de S. Paulo, puts Lula six points ahead of Flávio Bolsonaro in Brazil’s presidential race.

The poll, published on Friday 21 August 2026, shows Lula with 39% support against Flávio Bolsonaro’s 33% in the first round.

Datafolha Shows Lula Leading

Datafolha, the polling institute of the newspaper Folha de S. Paulo, published the survey on Friday 21 August 2026.

Fieldwork took place on Tuesday 18 and Wednesday 19 August 2026. The poll interviewed 2,058 voters aged 16 and over.

The margin of error is 2 percentage points.

First Round Numbers

In the first round, Lula has 39% and Flávio Bolsonaro 33%. That gives Lula a six-point lead, as the headline states.

However, the margin of error is 2 points, so the true gap could be as small as two points. Still, a six-point lead is outside the margin, so it is a reliable advantage.

Other Candidates Trail

The poll also tested other candidates in the first round. Ronaldo Caiado has 5%, Renan Santos 4%, and Romeu Zema 3%.

These numbers are far behind the top two. Therefore, the race appears to be a two-person contest.

Runoff Scenario

In a runoff against Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula leads 47% to 43%. This four-point gap is also within the margin of error.

Because the margin is 2 points, the runoff lead is not a sure thing. Even so, Lula holds a numerical advantage.

Government Approval Split

The poll also measured approval of the government. Approval stands at 47%, while disapproval stands at 50%.

This near-even split suggests a divided electorate. Meanwhile, the election is set for October 2026.

Poll Commissioned by Folha and TV Globo

Datafolha conducted the poll for Folha and TV Globo. It is registered with the electoral court, the TSE, under number BR-04496/2026.

This registration is standard for Brazilian polls. In addition, it ensures transparency.

Understanding the Margin of Error

A margin of error of 2 points means the true figure is likely within 2 points either side. A gap smaller than that is not a reliable lead.

For example, the runoff gap of 4 points is exactly twice the margin. Thus, it is a lead, but not a commanding one.

What Happens Next

Brazil’s presidential election is held in October 2026. If no candidate passes 50% in the first round, the top two go to a runoff.

Given the current numbers, a runoff seems likely. As a result, voters may see a second round between Lula and Flávio Bolsonaro.

Datafolha Methodology

The sample size is 2,058 voters aged 16 and over. The margin of error is 2 percentage points.

This methodology is standard for national polls. Overall, Datafolha provides a snapshot of voter intentions.

How many people were surveyed in this Datafolha poll?

The poll surveyed 2,058 voters aged 16 and over. The margin of error is 2 percentage points.

What are the first-round numbers in the Datafolha poll?

In the first round, Lula has 39% and Flávio Bolsonaro 33%. Other candidates trail far behind.

When is the Brazilian presidential election?

The election is in October 2026. If no candidate gets over 50%, the top two go to a runoff.

World.title: The Man in Black Opens His Archive: Pablo Ramírez on Memory, Tango and Buenos Aires
World.content:
In Archivo Ramírez, more than 700 previously unpublished images reveal the private processes behind one of Argentina’s most distinctive designers — and the city, music and memories that shaped his visual language.

BUENOS AIRES — Pablo Ramírez has spent more than 25 years building one of Argentina’s most recognizable design languages. It is a world of black and white, disciplined lines and controlled sensuality, clothing that seems restrained until the body moves and reveals a flash of skin, a white cuff or an unexpected trace of red.

Now, the famously exacting designer is allowing the public to see what usually remains outside the frame.

Archivo Ramírez, published in 2026 by Fundación Medifé Edita, opens his personal and professional archive through 256 pages and more than 700 previously unpublished images. Figurines, sketches, personal notebooks, technical sheets, travel memories, family albums, correspondence, runway records and fashion films form an intimate map of a career in which private memory and public work are inseparable.

The book is neither a conventional catalogue nor a glossy coffee-table retrospective. Conceived as a theoretical and visual essay, it preserves the drawings, tests, fragments and unfinished thoughts that precede the immaculate final image. Researcher Daniela Lucena coordinated its texts with Sebastián Rodríguez, Lorena Tenuta led the visual editing, and Estudio ZkySky created the editorial design.

At a June presentation at Teatro Dumont in Buenos Aires, Ramírez discussed the making of the archive with Lucena and Fundación Medifé Edita director Daniela Gutierrez. The conversation placed the book within a larger question: how does a nation preserve fashion not merely as commerce, but as cultural memory?

An Instinct to Save Everything

For Ramírez, the project began with a lifelong instinct to save things. He has kept diaries, scrapbooks, drawings and traces of the creative process since childhood. “This book is an extraordinary gift, something completely unexpected,” he has said. “It was always in my nature to save, to collect like treasure everything that passes through my hands during the work process: records of my life.”

The material documents an independent Argentine designer working through economic crises, cultural change and a fashion system increasingly driven by speed. It reveals not only what Ramírez made, but how he sustained an authorial identity.

From Navarro to Paris, and Back

Born in Navarro, in Buenos Aires Province, Ramírez moved to the capital to study fashion design at the University of Buenos Aires. His early professional path took him to Paris in 1994 to develop denim collections before he returned to Argentina and worked for established companies, including Alpargatas. A later period of unemployment led him to New York, where encounters with photographers and stylists encouraged him to stop waiting for permission and create a collection of his own.

The late stylist Dolores Navarro Ocampo gave him the decisive push. Ramírez recalled her telling him that it was time to make his collection. The result was Casta, presented in 2000 as part of the Grandes Colecciones series at the Sheraton Hotel. A study in chastity, religion and the black silhouette, Casta established the foundations of the visual vocabulary that would come to define his work.

Black became more than a colour choice; it was a method that removed distraction and directed attention toward proportion, construction and the wearer. As Ramírez has put it: “Black is pure silhouette. There is no distraction, it emphasizes the person wearing it.”

Tango, and the Turning Point

The following year, Ramírez turned toward a cultural language that had surrounded him since childhood. His second collection, Tango, was presented at Buenos Aires Fashion Week in 2001 and became an international turning point. “At home, we always listened to tango. My grandfather sang tango,” Ramírez recalled. He also remembers his grandfather’s distinctly tanguero elegance: the shirt, the hat and the polished shoes. Researching the collection led him back toward tango’s beginnings, particularly La Boca and the conventillos. “For me, tango has mystery and sensuality,” Ramírez said. “It also has elegance, and tango has a sophistication in its music and its dance that is very important to me.”

The collection did not reproduce one famous dancer, photograph or historical dress. Ramírez drew instead from music, memory, research and a constellation of images. What interested him was tango’s emotional architecture: tension, friction, melancholy, restraint and desire.

That sensibility appeared in garments that disclosed themselves gradually. White shirts interrupted the black. Red appeared inside a sleeve or lining, visible only when the wearer moved. Rather than repeat the international cliché of the red tango dress, Ramírez might reserve red for the lips or conceal it within the construction. “I am interested in something that initially appears closed or restrained and then suddenly allows the skin or a fragment of colour to appear,” he explained. “The sensuality comes from revelation, rather than from showing everything.”

Movement is embedded in his work even when it is not consciously planned. “The clothes I make, when people put them on, invite movement,” he said. As a boy, Ramírez wanted to be a dancer — an unrealized desire that may explain why his clothes do not merely sit on the body; they ask the wearer to inhabit them.

Isabella Blow, and an International Introduction

Tango also became the collection that carried Ramírez beyond Argentina. British fashion editor Isabella Blow attended the presentation, gave it a standing ovation and went backstage in tears. “She came backstage, started to cry and told me, ‘Look at me, I’m crying,’” Ramírez recalled. Blow said the collection had moved her, took pieces from the models and put them on. She then joined Michael Roberts for an impromptu shoot at Café Tortoni. The encounter transformed a deeply local story into an international introduction.

Afterward, international visitors often arrived already knowing his name through Tango. Argentine identity did not have to be diluted to travel; its specificity gave the work power.

Ramírez points to Claudio Segovia’s landmark stage production Tango Argentino as an earlier example of the same principle. The show reached Broadway by pairing refinement with authenticity: Segovia sought out genuine milonga dancers and musicians rather than inventing an artificial tango for export. “It was real, authentic and truthful,” Ramírez said, “but it was also presented with enormous sophistication.”

That union of truth and theatrical precision remains central to a career spanning more than 50 collections, international runways, opera, ballet, theatre, uniforms and music. Ramírez does not simply make clothes; he constructs characters and cultural worlds.

The City That Keeps the Archive Moving

If Archivo Ramírez preserves the past, Buenos Aires keeps the archive from becoming static. Ramírez has worked across Paris, Rome, São Paulo, Santiago and Montevideo, including costume design for Carmen at São Paulo’s Theatro Municipal. Yet he continues to describe the Argentine capital as an inexhaustible source. “Buenos Aires is an incredible city,” he said. “It is always changing. It is a mix, a mixture.”

The phrase could also describe the book. Behind the controlled black silhouette lies a dense network of family memories, travel, music, Catholic imagery, national history, stagecraft and urban contradiction. Archivo Ramírez makes that layered construction visible.

It also complicates the idea of a retrospective. Ramírez is not closing a chapter. His practice remains deliberately eclectic: he has designed Aerolíneas Argentinas uniforms, dressed musicians including Fito Páez and Gustavo Cerati, and created approximately 400 costumes for Carmen at São Paulo’s Theatro Municipal. In 2026 he returned to Teatro Solís in Montevideo to design Fidelio, Beethoven’s only opera. Recent projects also include restaurant uniforms in Recoleta and new stage work for Páez.

What the Archive Offers the Next Generation

The book’s deeper significance may be what it offers the next generation. By preserving drafts as carefully as finished dresses, Archivo Ramírez argues that creative process itself belongs to Argentina’s cultural history.

Ramírez is also open to returning to tango. Asked whether he could imagine a future project bringing fashion, music and dance together around the 20th anniversary of UNESCO’s inscription of tango in 2029, his answer was immediate: “I would love to.” The possibility points beyond a conventional runway toward a multidisciplinary cultural platform built from Argentine design, live music and dancers who carry tango as lived practice.

A return would not require repeating the 2001 collection. It could revisit its deeper proposition: tango is not a costume or tourist image, but a sophisticated living language capable of connecting Argentina with the world.

Ramírez’s career offers a pathway for a new generation of Argentine creatives: begin with what is unmistakably local, refine it until it becomes universal, and allow it to travel without erasing where it came from.

Archivo Ramírez may document more than three decades of work, but its most revealing pages are not monuments. They are traces of motion — drawings, fittings, revisions and memories that show an artist still becoming.

The boy who once wanted to dance ultimately found another way to choreograph the body. In black silhouettes shaped by Buenos Aires, the movement never stopped.

World.title: Batista Brothers to Buy Avibras, Brazil Missile Maker
World.content:
Brazil · DEFENCE

Key Facts — Deal date 21 August 2026

— Buyer J&F via Globe Investimentos

— Target Nova AVB S.A., holding of Avibras Aeroco

— Regulator CADE, Brazil’s antitrust authority

— Status Pending CADE approval

The purchase would put one of Brazil’s largest defence companies under the control of the family behind JBS, pending antitrust approval.

Illustrative photo: the Brazilian Aerospace Memorial at São José dos Campos. The sale of Avibras still needs approval from the antitrust regulator CADE. (Photo: Vrsooo, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.)

The Batista brothers are buying Avibras, Brazil’s missile maker, in a deal announced on 21 August 2026. J&F is the holding company of Joesley and Wesley Batista.

It agreed to acquire 100% of Nova AVB S.A., the holding that controls Avibras Aeroco.

A New Owner for Avibras

The Batista brothers are buying Avibras, Brazil’s missile maker, through their holding company J&F. The purchase was announced on 21 August 2026, with the transaction value not disclosed.

J&F will use its investment vehicle Globe Investimentos for the acquisition. This vehicle was also used for other industrial investments, including Usiminas.

What Avibras Does

Avibras Aeroco, formerly Avibras Indústria Aeroespacial, designs and makes artillery and defence systems, rockets, missiles and armoured vehicles. The company also produces multiple rocket launchers.

It is described as one of Brazil’s largest defence companies and a key supplier to the Army. In addition, Avibras keeps contracts with the Brazilian Army.

The Restructuring Background

Before this deal, control of Avibras sat with creditors through the Fundo Brasil Crédito. J&F had entered earlier as an investor and financier in the restructuring, not as controlling shareholder.

The old Avibras Indústria Aeroespacial, which holds the debts, remains in judicial recovery. Avibras Aeroco was created as a new operating structure holding the main industrial and technological assets.

Employees Informed

Employees were told through a formal company communication issued by Avibras Aeroco and Nova AVB on 21 August 2026. Unions relayed the news publicly.

The company said the sale had been submitted to antitrust review and was still pending completion. Therefore, the deal is not yet final.

Awaiting CADE Approval

The deal was formally notified to CADE, Brazil’s antitrust authority, and needs CADE approval before it can close. CADE said it does not comment on ongoing cases, and no approval had been granted at the announcement date.

As a result, the acquisition remains conditional on regulatory clearance. Even so, the announcement marks a significant step for Avibras.

The Batista Family’s Role

J&F is the holding company of the Batista family, Joesley and Wesley Batista. It controls JBS, one of the world’s largest meat companies.

In addition, J&F invests through vehicles such as Globe Investimentos. This purchase adds a defence firm to their portfolio.

Implications for Defence Policy

Coverage notes Avibras keeps contracts with the Brazilian Army and frames the deal as reviving debate about Brazil’s defence industrial policy. The sale could reshape how the country’s defence sector is owned.

However, the final outcome depends on CADE’s review. Until then, the future of Avibras under new ownership remains uncertain.

Understanding Judicial Recovery

Judicial recovery, recuperação judicial in Portuguese, is Brazil’s court-supervised process for restructuring a company’s debts. It is similar to Chapter 11 in the United States.

The old Avibras entity remains in this process, while the new operating company holds the core assets. This structure allowed J&F to inject capital into Avibras Aeroco.

Next Steps for Avibras

The sale of Avibras is pending completion, subject to CADE’s approval. Once approved, J&F would take full control of the missile maker.

Meanwhile, the company continues its operations and contracts. The deal, once final, would mark a new chapter for Avibras.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is buying Avibras?

The Batista brothers, Joesley and Wesley, through their holding company J&F, are buying Avibras. The acquisition is via Globe Investimentos, a J&F vehicle.

What does Avibras make?

Avibras designs and makes artillery and defence systems, rockets, missiles and armoured vehicles. It also produces multiple rocket launchers and is a key Army supplier.

Is the deal complete?

No, the deal is not complete. It needs approval from CADE, Brazil’s antitrust authority, before it can close.

What is judicial recovery?

Judicial recovery is Brazil’s court-supervised process for restructuring a company’s debts, similar to Chapter 11 in the US. The old Avibras entity remains in this process.

Sources: Company communication; CADE filings; Brazilian business press.

The Colombia earthquake has claimed 329 lives and left 247 people missing, according to the latest official count. The figures come from Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management, the UNGRD, reported on 22 August 2026.

The count has risen steadily since the quake.

The Colombia Earthquake in Numbers

The Colombia earthquake struck on the morning of 10 August 2026 in western Colombia. Its magnitude was 7.4, measured as moment magnitude by the United States Geological Survey and the Colombian Geological Service.

The epicentre was near San José del Palmar, in the department of Chocó, about three to five kilometres from the town. As of 22 August, the UNGRD reported 329 dead and 247 missing.

How the Toll Has Evolved

On the first day, 10 August, the toll was put at about 111 to 132 dead, with scores to about 570 injured. However, the numbers have changed as more information came in.

By 12 August, the US Embassy cited UNGRD figures of 181 dead, 2,754 injured and 189 missing. The same day, President Abelardo de la Espriella gave 265 dead, 496 missing and 3,494 injured.

On 13 August, Al Jazeera and Reuters reported 265 dead, nearly 500 missing and more than 3,500 injured. By 16 August, official estimates cited by Reuters gave around 290 dead, more than 140 missing and 4,200 injured.

Why the Numbers Differ

The differing counts come from different bodies counting at different moments. For example, the missing figure has moved up and down as people were found or newly reported.

Therefore, the latest verified injured count is from 16 August, with more than 4,200 injured. Meanwhile, the death toll has continued to climb.

Understanding Moment Magnitude

A moment magnitude is the modern measure of an earthquake’s total energy. Each whole number is about 32 times more energy released.

Each whole number on the scale means about 32 times more energy released.

The Epicentre and Region

The epicentre was near San José del Palmar, in the department of Chocó, about three to five kilometres from the town. Chocó is a western department of Colombia, known for its rugged terrain.

The quake’s location in a remote area has likely complicated response efforts. Still, the official toll continues to be updated.

Official Response and Reporting

The UNGRD is the main agency providing official figures. Reports from Reuters and Al Jazeera have tracked the evolving numbers.

In addition, the US Embassy has cited UNGRD figures, showing international attention. The Colombian president has also given his own counts.

The Human Impact

The Colombia earthquake has caused a significant loss of life. With 329 dead and 247 missing, many families are affected.

The injured count, as of 16 August, was more than 4,200. This shows the scale of the disaster.

Looking Ahead

The toll may still change as search and rescue operations continue. However, no current status of those operations has been verified.

Meanwhile, the focus remains on the affected communities in Chocó. The Colombia earthquake has left a deep mark on the region.

How to Help

For those wishing to assist, official channels like the UNGRD may provide guidance. However, no specific aid information is available at this time.

In short, the priority is supporting the survivors and the families of the missing. The Colombia earthquake is a tragedy that requires solidarity.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the latest death toll from the Colombia earthquake?

The latest official toll, from the UNGRD on 22 August 2026, is 329 dead and 247 missing. This figure has risen from earlier counts.

Where did the Colombia earthquake strike?

The earthquake struck near San José del Palmar, in the department of Chocó, western Colombia. The epicentre was about three to five kilometres from the town.

How strong was the Colombia earthquake?

The earthquake had a magnitude of 7.4, measured as moment magnitude. This was confirmed by the US Geological Survey and the Colombian Geological Service.

Why do the reported numbers for the Colombia earthquake vary?

Different agencies have reported different numbers at different times. The missing count has fluctuated as people are found or newly reported.

Sources: UNGRD; USGS; Reuters; Al Jazeera.

World.title: D’Fab 4 brings The Beatles Show to Lamanai Riverside Retreat
World.content:
D’Fab 4 brings The Beatles Show to Lamanai Riverside Retreat

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The Beatles are coming to Orange Walk, or as close as you can get.

D’Fab 4, a Beatles experience band, takes the stage live at Lamanai Riverside Retreat on Saturday, September 5 at 7pm.

The four piece delivers the songbook that defined a generation, from the early hits to the later work, played live by musicians who know the material inside out.

Saturday, September 5. Doors and music from 7pm at Lamanai Riverside Retreat.
